The story follows on directly from the animated film Justice League Dark: Apokolips War (2020), at the end of which Constantine persuaded the Flash to reset the timeline and undo the world-ending catastrophe. Constantine wakes up in the eerie House of Mystery with no memory of how or why he got there. To his relief, Zatanna and his friends are all there with him, but they have a bad habit of turning into demons and ripping him to shreds, and every time he dies he wakes up again to repeat the cycle. As he searches for the truth behind his imprisonment in the mansion, flashbacks reveal how his hellish trap is tied to the events of Apokolips War: for tampering with the fabric of reality, he has been cursed to spend eternity among the deadly threats inside the house, a punishment that the reviewer Max Byrne likened to that of Prometheus. True to the DC comic series The House of Mystery that inspired it, the short ends with a twist.

The short was well received. James Harvey of The World's Finest called it gripping, twisted and occasionally funny, arguably the strongest short in the collection, praising Ryan's performance, Peters's direction, Altbacker's story and Robert J. Kral's score. Max Byrne of Dark Knight News described it as a short, sharp shock, gory and delightfully evil, highlighting its horror-inspired score and voice cast. Sam Stone of CBR found it the most gruesome and somewhat out of place in an eclectic anthology, but always a delight for Ryan's return as the Hellblazer.

A prologue shows a group of people being chased through a forest by the mummy before performing a ritual that stops the creature and the "time loop" its awakening has created; the soldiers involved kill everyone connected with the incident. Some months later the British military hands the now dormant mummy to a university, where a group of archaeology students and their lecturer study it and learn about mummification and the creature's mysterious origins. When someone tries to steal the mummy's necklace, it rises again and begins stalking and killing those trapped inside the building. Its victims return as possessed servants who hunt down the survivors, and no one can escape, because time has frozen and anyone leaving one room finds themselves back where they started. The mummy needs to collect the souls of those who woke it in order to walk the earth for good, but the heroine discovers that it has only 24 hours to do so, and the survivors must stay alive until sunrise.

Phil Wheat of Nerdly found that the camp humour of the first film had been toned down in favour of a more traditional British mummy picture, but felt the film ended with a whimper as the survivors simply run out the clock, while leaving room for a third instalment. Don Anelli of Don's World of Horror and Exploitation called it enjoyable if flawed, praising the time-loop conceit, the practical, jerky-moving mummy and the creepy possessed followers, but finding the first half, dominated by classroom lessons on mummification, sluggish. One commenter also noted that the supposed university was evidently filmed in a secondary school.

In 2056, the environment has collapsed, nation states have given way to corporations with private armies, and only the rich can afford homes with clean air. Aboard the space station Rubikon, owned by the Nibra corporation, the scientist Dimitri Krylov has developed edible algae that produce oxygen. The corporate soldier Hannah Wagner arrives with Gavin Abbott, a chemist and heir to a powerful family, on a secret mission to bring the algae back to Earth. The rest of the crew, including Dimitri's son, departs for home but loses contact and burns up in the atmosphere amid debris created by eco-activists. Soon after, Hannah, Gavin and Dimitri watch as a brown toxic cloud engulfs the whole planet and all contact is lost.

Dimitri explains that the station's algae-based life support can sustain the three of them, but would fail if one of them died. Hannah discovers she is pregnant by Gavin, since her mandatory sterilization chip stopped working when the link to Earth went dead. When contact is restored, around three hundred corporate leaders and their families hiding in an underground bunker beg the crew to bring the algae down and save them. Hannah and Gavin want to return, but Dimitri sabotages their landing module, which explodes after they escape. Hannah then reveals that she was to send the algae culture down on an unmanned cargo shuttle, and the pair adapt it to carry people, until Hannah learns that the leaders sacrificed the soldiers who escorted them to the bunker and halts the launch. Gavin kills himself, believing that the others cannot survive alone and will have to return, but Dimitri admits he invented that danger to stop Gavin's earlier suicide attempt. Years later, Hannah's daughter picks up a radio signal revealing that some people have survived in southern camps.

Shot in a Vienna studio in late 2020, the film was presented at Karlovy Vary, opened the Kitzbühel festival and reached Austrian cinemas on 16 September 2022. Critics praised its visuals and production design but found it slow. It won Austrian Film Awards for production design and sound.

Emma, a French woman of African descent, finds welcome peace and color on a trip to the Dominican Republic, far from her gray life in France. Just as she is about to fly home, however, she is arrested for drug trafficking. After tense police interrogations, a fortuitous car accident allows her to escape, and she seeks refuge in one of the most dangerous districts of Santo Domingo. There she is taken in by three siblings who live on their own, since their mother is dead and their father is in prison. Only the youngest, Cuki, retains a childlike whimsy, while his sister T.I.N.A. and brother $hulo have hardened themselves to survive on the streets and keep their father's illicit business going. Hiding in their makeshift household, Emma longs to return home, but as Cuki grows ever more attached to her she becomes their protégée and a maternal figure, and the four form a family built on joy and hope amid the dangers outside. The children are curious about her Bantu heritage and the African diaspora, and she gleefully demonstrates the Maasai jumps Cuki once saw on television, as her destiny changes in unexpected ways.

"Girl in the Basement" is a psychological thriller television film that premiered on Lifetime in 2021. The movie follows the story of Sarah, a young woman who returns to her childhood home after being away for several years. She discovers that her mother has been living in the basement and claims she's been taking care of herself.

As Sarah tries to reconnect with her mother, she begins to uncover disturbing secrets about their family's past. Her mother reveals that she was involved in a cult-like group when Sarah was younger, and that she had been hiding from the outside world for years.

Sarah becomes increasingly unsettled as she learns more about her mother's past and the reasons behind her isolation. She starts to question everything she thought she knew about her family and their history. As tensions rise between Sarah and her mother, it becomes clear that there is more to the story than meets the eye.

Throughout the film, Sarah struggles with feelings of anger, betrayal, and confusion. Her relationship with her mother deteriorates as she tries to understand why her mother has been keeping such a dark secret from her for so long.

The movie takes a dark turn when it's revealed that Sarah's mother was involved in some sinister activities, including human trafficking and abuse. As the truth comes to light, Sarah is forced to confront the reality of her family's past and the harm that has been done.

Ultimately, "Girl in the Basement" is a gripping thriller that explores themes of trauma, family secrets, and the complexities of mother-daughter relationships. The film features strong performances from its cast, particularly the lead actress who brings depth and nuance to the complex character of Sarah.

The film follows three best friends in their mid-twenties, Sage (Gorman), Casey (Linez) and Morgan (Deckers), who are caught in the grip of quarter-life crises as they try to balance their careers and their love lives and stumble through the messy, embarrassing and confusing pitfalls of becoming adults. Sage is a talented graphic artist who spends her time complaining in a coffee shop, and the friends talk frankly about sex and lean on one another as each of them stalls on the way to true adulthood. Morgan's extracurricular activities eventually catch up with her, even as she falls in love with Lowick (Angel), a kind and ordinary man. Across the intersecting storylines the women's sexual encounters, from the absurd to the upsetting, serve as a springboard for exploring mental illness and the expectations society places on young people.

Umar Ali of The Upcoming found the film unabashedly crude and frank but said its script balances the ribald jokes with genuine pathos and strong character development; he praised the three leads for carrying the film where the screenplay falters and called it an ambitious, if rough-edged, and thoroughly entertaining exploration of adulthood. Shane A. Bassett of The People's Movies described it as a kind of millennial mumblecore romance that goes nowhere yet remains enlightening, singling out Deckers as the standout and comparing Gorman's potential to that of Greta Gerwig. Other reviewers felt the script was contrived and unfocused.

Laura Price (Hampele) is a high-powered San Francisco corporate lawyer on the verge of being made partner and engaged to the equally ambitious Owen (Horner). She grew up on the tropical island of Sapphire Cove with her best friends Chip and Gem, but has not seen them in years. When her firm's biggest client, Chip's grandfather, a business mogul who must cede control of his company before his 85th birthday, asks her to travel back to the island and get Chip to sign a contract making him his heir and a billionaire, she leaves her practice and her fiancé behind. Chip (McIntyre), however, is happily living on island time as the barefoot captain of a charter boat and ferry and wants nothing to do with the responsibility. The workaholic lawyer and the laid-back islander clash, haggle and strike bargains, such as his offer to read one page of the contract for every fun activity she tries on the island, and between emails, video meetings, pressure from her boss and distracted calls from Owen, Laura finds herself horse riding and snorkelling, rediscovering the place where she grew up and her feelings for Chip.

Critics found the film pleasant to look at but generic. Roger Moore of Movie Nation complained that the decision to scrub every trace of Australia from the film had bleached out its local colour and any chance of drama or romantic friction, calling it so dull that it barely passed Hallmark Channel muster, with a generic plot, bland characters and sleep-inducing dialogue, though he credited the leads for mastering American accents. Jane Freebury of The Canberra Times gave it two stars out of five, writing that it lacked wit and a sense of place. Other reviewers enjoyed its tropical scenery, breezy pace and the chemistry between Hampele and McIntyre.

Taylor, a Seattle research librarian who loves helping people dig up answers, loses her job when the library's funding is cut. Her brother Craig invites her for a change of pace to stay with his family in the small town of Forest Ridge, Montana, where he manages the historic, century-old Graff Hotel. On the way, her car ends up in a ditch and she is rescued by the handsome Joel, who knows the town, and sparks fly. In Forest Ridge she learns that the Graff has been bought by a tech tycoon and his associate Ray Dixon, who plan to turn the quaint hotel into an upscale property for tourists, a scheme that divides the town. At a town hall meeting she discovers that the tycoon is Joel himself, back in his hometown to push the project forward, despite his father's warning that the residents will resist. Determined to protect the hotel's charm and her brother's job, Taylor points out that the Graff could qualify for landmark status, which would prevent the city council from issuing renovation permits, if she can prove that a significant historical event took place there. As the two spend time together, an attraction grows between them even as their loyalties pull them apart. With the clock ticking, Taylor finds a photograph that could establish the property's historical value while also revealing an invaluable piece of personal history for its new owner.

The film was received as a gentle, clean seasonal romance. Rissi JC of RissiWrites found it sweet and cozy despite a familiar plot, praising the realistic chemistry in what she counted as at least the third pairing of Lowndes and Murray. The Dove Foundation approved it for all ages, describing a slow-burning love story with a twist at the end.

At the dawn of chaos, the first demon in the world, Yuandi, was born and came to be worshipped as the ancestor of all demons, once ruling the three realms before being imprisoned. Thousands of years later, the former demon king Sun Wukong, freed from beneath the Five Elements Mountain by the monk Tang Sanzang, travels west with his master and fellow disciples Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing in search of scriptures. When the group stops to rest at a temple, the ever-hungry Bajie talks Wukong into hunting for a legendary food treasure, and the two roughly plunder a sacred tree. Unknown to them, the tree marks the top of Yuandi's prison, and their recklessness sets the demon free. Escaping, Yuandi takes Master Tang captive. Wukong, Bajie and Wujing set out to rescue their master and defeat the demon for good, accompanied by Fruity, the embodiment of the qi energy that had sealed Yuandi away. Along the way Wukong dispatches a series of foes with strength and cunning, but must find within himself the power to face the truly formidable Yuandi, while Master Tang's Buddhist teaching of equality is set against the demon's desire to dominate others.

The film was released in Chinese theaters on 2 April 2021. Well Go USA, which had previously handled the animated films Ne Zha and Jiang Ziya, distributed it in North America, releasing it on Blu-ray, DVD and digital platforms on 7 December 2021 with an English-language audio track. Reviews praised its spectacle but criticized its writing. Douglas Davidson of Elements of Madness gave it three out of five, calling the inventive action sequences great fun and never dull while describing the script as flimsy, the characters undeveloped and the tone wildly uneven, mixing crude humor aimed at younger viewers with violence suited to teenagers and older audiences, and comparing many of the CG fights to extended video game cutscenes.

Set a year after the first film, the story follows Bodi, the guitar-playing dog from the village of Snow Mountain, whose power-pop trio True Blue has become the hottest new act in the city, its music radiating waves of blue energy over its fans. The band attracts the attention of Lang, a music-impresario sheep with a fluffy pompadour and a British Invasion accent, who invites them on tour with the pop sensation Lil' Foxy. Lang has hidden agendas: he wants to separate Bodi from his bandmates, to shut down Rock'n'Roll Park, where the city's diehard rockers keep the flame burning, and to harness Bodi's musical energy with a special machine so that he can hypnotise crowds of musicians into his zombie-like followers. Meanwhile, back in Snow Mountain, Bodi's family fret about his sudden fame while profiting from True Blue merchandise, and an avalanche strikes the village. Bodi has to learn the price of fame and how to stay true to himself, his roots and his friends.

Phil Hoad of The Guardian called it a hectic sequel with an all-over-the-place plot, mixing celebrity satire and a nostalgic Asian rural fable with a Zootopia-style city and references from Bill & Ted to the Rolling Stones; he found the animation cheaper and stiffer than the original's and the satire generic, but thought it worldly enough to intrigue pre-teens and credited its finale with a demented energy. Common Sense Media recommended it from age six, praising its messages about self-worth, family, teamwork and humility.

The documentary presents Kabini as a kingdom home to rival confederations of animals vying for dominance, among them tigers, wild dogs and resident leopards. Saya, the only black panther in the forest, challenges the status quo by staking his claim to the throne. He must adapt to a dry deciduous habitat that is bone-dry for half the year, where his black coat makes him stand out among brown undergrowth and absorbs heat faster than a spotted leopard's. He learns to use shadows, climbing trees with dense canopies and dark bark to hide and hunt, and unlike other leopards he relishes the monsoon rains. The film follows him hunting, drinking and fighting for territory as he confronts Scarface, the fearsome alpha male, and courts Cleopatra, the dominant female; at the end Saya finds a mate and the pair settle together in their territory.

First spotted in 2015, Saya had been followed by Jung for years before he approached National Geographic in 2017 with footage and a basic script. The commission brought a filming permit that allowed the crew, working from two vehicles with the help of the Karnataka Forest Department, to spend around ten hours a day in the park for three years, often glimpsing the cat for only seconds. In 2018 the team went 81 days without a sighting before Saya reappeared with a deer fawn in his mouth. Binoo K. John of The Federal praised the film's brilliant photography and heart-tugging first-person storytelling, suggesting it could rank as the best wildlife documentary ever shot in India.

Gabriel (Moss) is a gentle, kind seven-year-old Chinese-American first-grader who takes ballet lessons, plays with dolls and loves the colour pink. At school he befriends Rob (Hu), a sporty boy who has recently moved to the United States from China and who is mocked by classmates because of the smell of the Chinese food he brings for lunch. After some hesitation Rob comes to enjoy his new friend's company and encourages him rather than trying to change him. Rob's father, however, grows suspicious of Gabriel's feminine interests and decides to intervene, confronting Gabriel's parents over dinner, who respond by accepting their son exactly as he is.

Peng, who identifies as non-binary and grew up in China, based the story on an incident from their own childhood, when a neighbour's father came to the family's dinner table to tell Peng's father that his child was not normal and needed to be fixed, and Peng's father defended them. In an interview with Laughing Place, Peng said the film was meant to encourage viewers to stay open-minded and curious about people who are different rather than rushing to judgement, explained that both boys' most painful moments take place while eating as a way of linking their experiences of being othered, and described a nationwide search before Moss was cast. Alex Reif of Laughing Place called it a charming short about not being afraid to be oneself, likely to resonate deeply with LGBTQ+ viewers, and Franck Armand-Zuniga of Chronique Disney found it particularly moving, praising the two young actors for conveying overwhelming emotion.

Walter is a grumpy family man who cannot stand noise. His stressful work routine leads to a nervous breakdown, and at the hospital he learns that his hearing is literally hanging by a thread and that the next loud noise could be fatal. On medical advice, he and his wife Joana sell everything, leave Rio de Janeiro and buy a house in a small mountain town, hoping to find peace and quiet surrounded by nature. Their plans for a tranquil life are shattered, however, when they meet their new neighbor, Toninho, a good-natured man who loves throwing parties and is the drum master of a samba school. He holds samba rehearsals at home, and his children practice drums and tuba in the garden. A war breaks out over which will prevail in the neighborhood, noise or silence, as Walter's increasingly desperate attempts to silence the household next door clash with Toninho's carefree lifestyle. Amid music, arguments and very different ways of living, the two neighbors and their families must eventually learn to coexist.

Fenced In premiered on Netflix on 1 September 2022. Critical reception was mixed to negative. CinePOP felt that the comedy rarely got laughs, finding Walter too abrasive for viewers to sympathize with and the conflict essentially one-sided, while praising the colorful sets, costumes and lighting and Manfrini's adorably irritating performance; it also noted a recreation of the famous Porta dos Fundos sketch that made Rabello a viral sensation. Omelete criticized a script made up of incoherent scenes while acknowledging the talent of the cast, A Gazeta considered the film unoriginal but effective thanks to the chemistry between Hassum and Manfrini, and UOL Splash was much more negative, objecting to its humor and its many jokes.

Nina (Cordeiro), an aspiring digital influencer, discovers that a video of her famous boyfriend cheating on her has gone viral. To get over the break-up, she uses her contacts to land an all-expenses-paid trip to Salvador during Carnival week, invited by the charming singer Freddy Nunes (Borges), and brings along her three best friends: the crowd-shy Mayra (Inocencio), the nerdy, guarded Vivi (Pascotto) and the loud, flirtatious Michelle (Kayane). On arrival, they find themselves in a poor hotel with fewer privileges than the more famous influencers. Desperate to climb the social media ladder, Nina neglects her friends to chase likes and Freddy's attention. Vivi is courted by a fellow geek, Samir (Medrado), and the popular influencer Luana (Pavanelli) courts cancellation after drunken offensive remarks. Salvador (Pedro), a local tour guide who develops a crush on Nina, shows her the city away from the sponsored Carnival floats and teaches her to enjoy the moment rather than live behind a phone screen. A late twist involves a character trying to pass as straight, whom one of the friends supports when the truth comes out. Each of the women learns something about herself, and Nina realises that social media fame is a poor substitute for real friendship.

Set in Japan's Taishō era, the story follows Tanjiro, a kind-hearted boy who supports his family by selling charcoal in a town below their snowy mountain home. Returning one day, he finds his family slaughtered by a demon; only his younger sister Nezuko survives, but she has been turned into a demon herself. The Demon Slayer Giyu Tomioka arrives to kill her, but Tanjiro defends her, and when Nezuko resists her craving for human flesh, Giyu spares them and sends Tanjiro to the trainer Sakonji Urokodaki on Mount Sagiri. After burying their family, the siblings set out. Urokodaki tests Tanjiro's resolve and accepts him as a pupil, and over two years Tanjiro learns Total Concentration and Water Breathing, aided by the mysterious swordsmen Sabito and Makomo, former students of Urokodaki, until he cuts a giant boulder in two. At the Final Selection, a seven-day ordeal on a mountain full of captive demons, he defeats the Hand Demon, which had killed Sabito, Makomo and other students of his master. Tanjiro returns as one of only a handful of survivors, reunites with an awakened Nezuko, receives a sword that turns black and is sent on his first mission to a village where young girls have been disappearing.

Sibling's Bond played in Japanese theaters for two weeks from 29 March 2019, a week before the television premiere on 6 April. Aniplex of America screened it at the Aratani Theatre in Los Angeles on 31 March 2019, and Madman Entertainment presented it in select Australian theaters on 2 April. The series' opening theme, "Gurenge," is performed by LiSA, and Aniplex of America licensed the anime for streaming in North America.

Jose (Diosdado) considers David (Mestanza) the man of his life, so when David suddenly breaks up with him after eight years together, he struggles to move on. Some months after the separation, the two men, who have not seen each other since, agree to meet again on La Palma, the island where they first met. Their reunion turns into a road trip around the island in which they attempt something like a second honeymoon, while also throwing old resentments in each other's faces. As Jose is haunted by memories of their past, he begins to realise that their life together was not as ideal as he had believed, and the trip exposes the emotional dependence of one partner and the evasiveness of the other, their experiments with an open relationship and the infidelities that came with it, and the fear of loneliness that keeps them tied to a love that may already be over.

The film was poorly received by Spanish critics. Miguel Ángel Pizarro of eCartelera gave it 3 out of 10, calling it a failed debut and a jumble of ideas that tries at once to be a drama of heartbreak, a Call Me by Your Name-style celebration of its natural landscapes and a defence of open relationships, while sacrificing coherence in its characters' actions; he praised the chemistry between Mestanza and Diosdado but felt the actors could not save a tedious film that recalled the low-budget niche gay cinema of the late 1990s. Salvador Llopart of La Vanguardia gave it one star out of five, describing a clumsy island road movie that wants to be both physical and sentimental but ends up resembling an advertisement, and decine21 rated it 1 out of 10.

According to the legend, the Queen of Spades can be summoned by drawing a door and a staircase on a mirror in lipstick and ordering her three times to show herself. If the rite is performed correctly, the specter appears and grants a wish, but she is often more inclined to harm those who call her. In Ottawa, four teenage friends watch a young man jump to his death from a rooftop, muttering "Queen of Spades" as he dies. Curious rather than shaken, they research the legend online and find instructions for the ritual, which says the youngest member of the group must perform it, so thirteen-year-old Anna is chosen. At first nothing seems to happen and they carry on with their lives, but soon they experience disturbing visions and strange events, and one of the boys discovers a mysterious bloody gash on his arm before dying of a heart attack. When Mary, a single mother whose child is among the group, learns about the rite, she seeks out Smirnov, a Russian expert in the supernatural who has written a book about the legend, hoping he can stop the Queen from claiming more victims. Smirnov's attempts include trying to transfer the demon's spirit into a cat.

Queen of Spades was released on video on demand in the United States and Canada in June 2021. Reviews were mixed to negative. Matt Patti of Film Festival Today gave it two and a half stars out of four, finding it unoriginal and burdened by weak early dialogue and rushed exposition, but an effective paranormal horror film with genuinely frightening jump scares and a creepy demon design. Eric Hillis of The Movie Waffler was far harsher, calling it lacklustre low-budget horror that reduces the legend to a third-rate Candyman knockoff with unremarkable deaths and a lazily designed demon, though he felt Ohm gave a performance worthy of a far better movie.

Having fought its way through all seven Singularities that threatened human history, the Chaldea Security Organization at last reaches the endpoint of the Grand Order: the Final Singularity, the Grand Temple of Time, a domain created by Solomon, the King of Magic, who intends to destroy the world. As the final operation looms, Romani Archaman weighs the choices he will soon have to make, Mash Kyrielight reflects on the limits of her own life, and the Master Ritsuka Fujimaru prepares to receive a new Mystic Code. The pair then launch their last mission into the temple, where dozens of Heroic Spirits they have met over the course of their journey arrive to join the battle against Solomon's forces, in a final struggle to reclaim humanity's future.

Kim Morrissy of Anime News Network gave the film a B, likening it to the Avengers: Endgame of the Fate franchise because its appeal hinges on cameos from dozens of Servants rarely seen in animated form. She admitted the plot was a load of nonsense she loved every minute of, praised the animation by the Babylonia team as among the best-looking in the franchise and the satisfying climax and ending, which neatly wraps up the first part of the story, but found the theatrical dialogue potentially cheesy and self-indulgent, the ensemble action scenes too short and the film likely to be off-putting to viewers who had not played the game.

The film moves between two time frames, intercutting the story of the marriage with the police investigation after Jennifer vanishes. Jennifer, a thoughtful aspiring novelist from a very wealthy New York family, and the gregarious, athletic Fotis first met at Brown University but begin a whirlwind romance years later and marry within a year, as Jennifer, then 35, longs for a family. Her friends, especially Audrey, suspect he is after her money. Fotis bankrolls a struggling development company with her family's wealth and spends much of the year away on business and skiing trips while Jennifer, raising their five children largely alone with the help of a nanny, puts aside her writing. He belittles her, flies into rages and makes threats, and eventually openly brings his mistress Michelle into their life, telling Jennifer to accept it. She files for divorce and moves out with the children, leading to a bitter custody battle in which Fotis threatens to take the children to Greece and to kill her. When Jennifer disappears in New Canaan, Audrey points the police towards Fotis, and investigators reconstruct how they believe he attacked her in her garage and cleaned up with rolls of paper towels, tracing his movements on security cameras even though her body is never found. Fotis, charged with her murder, takes his own life while still protesting his innocence, and Michelle is charged as well.

Reviews were broadly favorable. TV Fanatic praised its respectful focus on Jennifer's life, Gish's grace in the role and Christie's balance of charm and volatility. Mark Gabrish Conlan of Movie Magg found it well made and eloquently acted, especially by Gish. Beverly White of MEAWW called it a fascinating cautionary tale and praised Christie, though she found Gish oddly relaxed at times.

The Titans are relaxing by the pool at Titans Tower when a spaceship lands and the Nerdlucks, the small aliens who tried to kidnap Michael Jordan and the Looney Tunes in Space Jam, step out carrying a VHS copy of the film. Robin is convinced they are evil, but the others overrule him and invite them in. Astonished to discover that his teammates have never seen Space Jam, Cyborg organises a watch party. As the film plays, Raven and Starfire supply running commentary, with Starfire pointing out plot holes, Cyborg presents fun facts, Beast Boy keeps count of the film's many butt shots, and Robin keeps a suspicious eye on the guests. When the movie shows the Nerdlucks stealing the talents of NBA players, the Titans pause it and, apart from Robin, let the visitors try the trick on them: Blanko takes Cyborg's powers, Bupkus Raven's, Bang Beast Boy's and Nawt Starfire's, while Pound is left unchanged because Robin has no powers to give. As the screening continues, the question is whether the Nerdlucks have come for an innocent party or have something more sinister in mind.

New animated sequences of the Titans are spliced into the archive footage, which features Michael Jordan, Wayne Knight, Bill Murray and Billy West as Bugs Bunny. Much of the original was trimmed for time, and its well-known songs were replaced with other music, apparently for licensing reasons.

Reviewers found the premise fun but the execution unbalanced. It's A Stampede! praised the humour of the Titans' commentary and its jokes about parts of Space Jam that have aged badly, but felt there was too much of the old film and too little new Titans material, leaving a hybrid that works fully as neither.

A remote area of the Welsh mountains has been abandoned for years because of radiation; no one knows why, and no one dares to enter. When a pair of vloggers venture into the hills, they discover the reason when they are burned alive by a dragon. The army calls in Vanessa Reid and her small team of special operatives to investigate the creature. Her unlikely team consists of two women, one of them injured and on crutches and the other soon developing a strange illness that may be linked to the dragons and to the radiation on the mountainside. The trio meet Professor Palson and his assistant Nicole, who clearly know more about what is happening in the mountains than they admit. Most of the action unfolds indoors as a dragon egg prepares to hatch, people begin losing their minds and tensions erupt among the group. A small dragon returns at the end, the creatures turn out to have evolved from the traditional dragon form into something more bird-like, and a closing scene hints at a much larger dragon to come.

The film was scheduled for release in the United Kingdom in September 2021. Reviews were negative. Phil Wheat of Nerdly gave it two out of five, noting that there were few furious dragons in Dragon Fury and that most of its running time was taken up with talk, although he credited thoughtful details in the sparingly used computer-generated effects, such as the dragons casting shadows, and their unusual bird-like design. Ade Smith of Movies & Mania found it a mostly dull drama after a promising opening in a rugged landscape, criticizing its implausible trio of operatives and silly final reveal while praising Wright's performance and Reichental's score. Voices from the Balcony called the computer effects variable, the dragon itself cool-looking, and the plot predictable.

The title refers both to the setting and to a secret underground game show staged there and streamed for the entertainment of the rich. A prologue reveals the game's twisted secret: its contestants are hunted by dinosaurs and there is no real way out. Sienna (Wunna), a down-on-her-luck mother desperate to win the large cash prize, signs up without knowing what the game involves and brings her two children along with her. At the hotel a floating orb relays the commands of the unseen Games Master, informing the women that their phones will not work and that the dinosaurs will try to kill them; whoever survives the night will win. While the other contestants are picked off one by one, Sienna's children wander off to explore before the game begins, venturing into a cave on the property, and her need to keep them safe gives her an edge as she fights to stay alive. One sequence echoes the famous kitchen scene from Jurassic Park, with raptors loose alongside one of her children.

Reviews were negative. Phil Wheat of Nerdly gave it two and a half stars out of five, describing it as Jurassic Park meets Escape Room and the weirdest game show ever conceived; he found the computer-generated dinosaurs fake-looking, the other contestants generic stereotypes and the premise unexplained, noting that Jurassic Games had told a similar story better, though he considered it better than some bigger-budget reality-TV horror films. Ade Smith of Movies & Mania thought the dinosaurs added novelty and the running time was agreeably short, but saw a distinct lack of suspense and urgency and weak acting. Other reviewers criticised its sparse attack scenes and poorly integrated effects.

Zooza, known as Z (List), Rob (Meyer), Courtney (Mawema) and Cotton (Santa Juana) are close friends in a small town who are at a turning point in their lives as they prepare to leave for college. While browsing at a yard sale, Z and Cotton come across a strange orb-like object, and the ominous woman selling it tells them that it is "the Friendship Game", which tests true friendship by having the players reveal their deepest desires. Unfazed, they buy it, and all four friends place their fingers on the object and confess what they most want. Their wishes come at an unexpected cost that begins to consume their lives: at a party soon afterwards, Cotton tries to warn the others that something is wrong, discovers Z and Rob together and storms off, and then disappears, prompting a police investigation. Meanwhile Kyle (Schombing), who spends most of his time at his computer, has been secretly watching the four friends, and the film increasingly blurs the digital and physical worlds with glitching, warped imagery. Told in chapters from each character's perspective, the story shows how the game sets the friends against one another with increasingly destructive consequences the deeper they go.

Reviews were largely negative, although Peyton List's performance was widely praised. Chase Hutchinson of Collider likened the premise to Wish Upon (2017) and felt the film gestured at the existential, internet-age concerns of We're All Going to the World's Fair, but said that, despite some occasionally enrapturing visuals, it spun its wheels and leaned on conventional scares that failed to land. Bobby LePire of Film Threat called it awful on every level except for List, who he said made the cringe-inducing dialogue believable and was the only cast member to inject real drama or fear, while criticising the rest of the cast, singling out Meyer for lacking screen presence. Screen Rant described it as a frustrating horror mystery that felt like a messy rough draft.

In the Brazilian Amazon, the anthropologist Nicholas Kieran unearths a statue holding a striking green triangular relic. When a member of his team proposes selling it, a piercing sound rings out and swarms of insects attack the dig. Learning that their father is missing, his children Amanda and Scott set off to find him. Amanda hires the boat of Captain Lebecq, who agrees to take her upriver along with Vera, a woman claiming to be in charge of the excavation, and Scott jumps aboard at the last moment. Guided by Lebecq and his crewmen Sark and Teese, the group goes ashore, where poison dart frogs attack Lebecq. As Sark prepares to cut off his leg, a seemingly blind stranger emerges from the forest, treats the wound and warns them of the Curupira, an indigenous deity who fiercely protects the rainforest and dwells at the heart of the jungle.

Pressing on, the travelers lose Teese to piranhas that wreck their boat, and are scattered by crocodiles. Amanda and Lebecq reach the abandoned dig and escape an attack by bullet ants, while Nicholas, the sole survivor of his team, is revealed to be living in a trailer with the relic. Captured by a tribe of cannibals who mistake Scott for one of the loggers destroying the forest, the group escapes when giant spiders drop from a sacred tree and attack their captors. Following clues left by the blind man, Amanda deduces that the heart of the jungle is a waterfall, behind which giant snakes swallow her companions; she cuts her way out and frees all but Sark. Outside they find the dying Lebecq and their father bound nearby. When the Curupira, a huge two-legged creature with flames on its back, appears, they destroy the relic to free it, while Vera tries to shoot the deity and is devoured by a giant Venus flytrap. The family heads home as the Curupira watches over the forest.

Released on 25 June 2021, the film received poor reviews. German critics mocked its cheap effects, simple story and childish dialogue, though some singled out Gorske's committed performance and the film's ecological message.

Misael (Leguizamo), an ordinary man, is locked up in the squalid jail of his small town after killing a man in a crime of passion, believing he was avenging the abuse of one of his children. After he strikes Cáceres (Rodríguez), the head of the guards, on arrival, the guard becomes fixated on him, and Misael is systematically beaten, tortured, humiliated and sexually abused by guards and fellow inmates. Blamed and forgotten by his loved ones, he is tormented above all by his separation from his family and his need for his son to understand why he did what he did. A lawyer (Barraza) takes up his case, and during a conjugal visit his wife (Sinisterra) confesses her infidelity and tells him he was wrong about the man he killed. In his loneliness Misael finds tenderness only in Sarna, a stray dog that lives in the prison and becomes his one faithful companion.

Trompetero, known mainly for popular comedies, said the project took more than seven years and was a cathartic, personal departure for him. It was filmed in an abandoned prison in Facatativá, near Bogotá, after research in prisons such as La Picota, and used former guerrilla and paramilitary fighters as extras. Oswaldo Osorio of the Cinéfagos blog at El Colombiano called it a strong, aggressive film of dirty realism that explores human misery through a forgotten man, praising the use of Sarna as a leitmotif. Carlos Giraldo of El Sabanero X rated it four out of five, calling it sordid, cruel and pessimistic and praising Barraza, but noted that some viewers considered its portrayal of the homosexual guard homophobic.

The story is set in a remote wilderness preserve that offers a big-game safari experience in which wealthy thrill-seekers pay for the privilege of hunting genetically recreated dinosaurs with rifles, arrows and grenades. Parker, the only woman in a new group of otherwise male trophy hunters that includes Torres (Pla) and Valentine (Dospil), is not what she seems: she is an undercover activist, and a vegan, trying to gather evidence to expose the operation. Lindon, the ambitious and ruthless tycoon who runs the park, is determined to keep it secret from the outside world. Soon after the party sets out, their guide is killed by raptors, and the hunters find themselves picked off one by one by the animals they came to kill, in encounters with a pterodactyl, a stampeding Tyrannosaurus and wave after wave of baby raptors. As the survivors try to escape the park, Lindon, who suspects Parker of being a spy, makes no effort to rescue them, appearing instead to cheer on the dinosaurs, and sends a hit squad after her.

Reviewers found the film cheap but not without entertainment value. Writing for Free Kittens Movie Guide, D. M. Anderson said the computer-generated effects were on a par with a student project and the film looked hastily slapped together, with laughable lapses in logic and continuity, yet found it surprisingly entertaining and sometimes genuinely funny without heavy-handed self-awareness, singling out Torbert's mercenary Blackhawk, whose monologue about the power of killing is cut short by a pterodactyl. Jim McLennan of Film Blitz gave it a C, saying it had surpassed his low expectations; he felt the dinosaur effects passed muster on their own but not when interacting with the actors, criticised its pixelated digital blood and thin characters, but enjoyed the scene in which a hunter faces a horde of baby raptors.

June works at a hospital but dreams of becoming a writer, while Rick is a successful author whose latest novel has just made the New York Times bestseller list and whose female readers adore him. He wants to celebrate by starting a family, but June wants to finish her first novel before having children, and she complains to her sister Maggie that Rick does not take her ambitions seriously. One day June finds a blackmail letter in the mail from a woman who claims Rick sexually assaulted her and demands 50,000 dollars, or she will go to the police and go public. Rick insists that he is innocent and that obsessive fans make such claims; fearing that in the MeToo era even a false accusation could end his career, June persuades him to pay, using his bonus check. Rick then argues that his high profile makes it too risky for him to deliver the money, so June agrees to make the drop herself. At night in a parking garage she finds the blackmailers, Wendy Bach, whom she had seen bruised at the hospital the day before, and her husband Simon, stabbed to death in their car. She flees home in a blood-stained coat, which Rick promises to burn. Instead, when the police arrive with evidence suggesting June had an affair with Simon, the briefcase of money turns out to contain her bloody coat and the murder weapon. Arrested, injured and handcuffed to a hospital bed, with even her sister doubting her, June escapes, crashes her car into a river and is presumed dead. Free to investigate, she discovers that her husband leads a deadly double life, using a disguise and an alias on dating apps to meet and assault women, while he also pursues Maggie. Using apps, trackers and the media, June sets out to expose him.

Reviews were mixed. That Darn Girl Movie Reviews gave it five out of five, calling it one of Lifetime's best framed-woman films for its fast start and handling of MeToo themes, though it found the villain's final monologue ridiculous. The novelist Tina Martin found the concept unoriginal and June's choices implausible.

In a snowy prologue, the wealthy widow Helen hounds Kelly, a pregnant young woman whom she insists is her daughter. Fleeing Helen's house, Kelly is killed when she loses control of her car while answering her phone, and when the police come to question Helen she stabs an officer and is committed to a mental hospital. Some nine months later Helen is back in the same house, and Sarah and Kyle, a young couple, move in next door. Helen's own daughter took her life years before, and since then Helen has fixated on young women in troubled marriages who are about to have children, trying to recast them as her family. Sarah, who grew up in a group home with Jennifer and was never adopted, is drawn to Helen's warmth, confiding that Kyle once had an affair, and when she learns she is pregnant Helen celebrates with her like a mother. When Grace, the social worker monitoring her, discovers Helen's shrine to her past obsessions, Helen stabs her and buries her in the snow, and she later kills Judith, who has grown suspicious and found out about Helen's past online. With Kyle often away on business, Helen bribes Angela to set him up in compromising photographs, and Sarah, believing he is cheating again, leaves him. Helen then takes her to a remote country house she has bought, drugs her and holds her captive, intending to raise Sarah and the baby as an all-female family. Jennifer finds the property's address in Helen's trash and Grace's buried body, and Kyle races to rescue his wife as Helen opens fire with a gun.

Mark Gabrish Conlan of Movie Magg considered it better done than most Lifetime films of its type, praising Romano's quick, economical setup, Yang's suspenseful direction and Grover's deliciously unsubtle, full-throated performance. Patrick Serrano of Lifetime Uncorked recapped it with enthusiasm, lamenting the death of Judith.

A prologue shows firefighter Theo Abrams (Geduld) and his colleagues battling a catastrophic blaze in a Cape Flats township, where he defies protocol to rescue a baby from a burning home, with tragic consequences that later return to him in flashbacks. Months afterwards he is suspended from his job, suffering from severe post-traumatic stress disorder and dulling it with alcohol rather than through his mandatory therapy sessions. His relationship with his wife Angela (Fortuin), a journalist, is strained, and she has warned him, after a tip from a mysterious informant, that he is in danger. One morning, after an argument, Theo wakes up to find her strangled beside him, with no memory of what happened and the evidence pointing to him. Disbelieved by police detective Rene Williamson (Mabalane) and pursued by deputy police chief Alan Shard, who is determined to catch him before he retires, he escapes when a police van crashes and, while on the run, investigates a conspiracy linked to the shadowy defence contractor M-Tech, which appears to be targeting a list of seemingly unconnected people.

Reviews were generally favourable about the action and less so about the script. Variety praised the sharp fight choreography and stunt work, including an extended hotel-room escape, and Geduld's charismatic performance in moments of panic and rage, but found the dialogue flat and declarative, likened the plot to The Fugitive, The Bourne Identity and The Manchurian Candidate, and felt the late turn into light science fiction strained the budget. Noel Murray of the Los Angeles Times wrote that the weight of exposition dragged down a strong premise, while the German critic Christopher Diekhaus singled out Geduld's intensely physical performance.

The film traces Schumacher's path from karting to the top of motorsport. It shows the modest family restaurant beside his father Rolf's kart track in Kerpen and reveals that the young Michael raced on worn tyres fished out of the bins of better-off rivals, while his brother Ralf recalls the two boys driving on slicks in the rain. Rolf describes the moment his son received his first professional contract from manager Willi Weber. Schumacher's reaction to the death of Ayrton Senna in 1994 is explored through an interview in which he admits he was sleeping perhaps three hours a night. The film covers his collision with Jacques Villeneuve in the 1997 title decider at Jerez and his crash with David Coulthard in 1998, and his years at Ferrari, where Jean Todt admits that management once wondered whether Mika Häkkinen would be the better driver, before Ferrari's run of drivers' titles from 2000 to 2004. Corinna and Todt portray a man who was shy, self-doubting and suspicious of strangers behind his public image, but also a man who loved a party.

The final part turns to the skiing accident in Méribel in December 2013. The family reveals that he had briefly considered going skydiving in Dubai instead. Without disclosing details of his condition, Corinna says he is still there, different but there, receiving therapy at home, and Mick, now himself a Formula One driver, says he would give up everything to be able to talk motorsport with his father. Other interviewees include his daughter Gina-Maria, Sebastian Vettel, Damon Hill, Bernie Ecclestone and Flavio Briatore.

Shang-hai (Guo), a celebrated mixed martial arts champion, swore never to fight again after an opponent died during one of his matches, and retired to run his family's international business. Mai Wen (Yoo), a rising fighter on his way to becoming a champion, must first defeat one of Shang-hai's students and Shang-hai's best friend, and he falls in love with Shang-hai's sister. Meanwhile Jessica (Zhu), a shady woman who turns out to be part of a drug-smuggling ring, approaches Mai Wen with her own plans. When the bout ends with the death of his friend under suspicious circumstances, Shang-hai has no choice but to step back into the ring, despite his sister's pleas, to uncover the truth. A much larger conspiracy centred on Jessica emerges, and Mai Wen is revealed to be an undercover police officer. The fights include an underground cage surrounded by crocodiles, and the story moves between brightly coloured seaside locations.

Reviews were largely negative. Panos Kotzathanasis of Asian Movie Pulse felt the film prized impression over substance to the point of losing all sense of measure, criticising a nonsensical script, the English dubbing of an already mediocre cast of bodybuilders and models, and choreography slowed by its bulky stars, though he admired its look and Zhu's femme fatale. Derrick Dunn of Reviews & Dunn gave it a D-, crediting only the opening fight between Guo and Greene and calling the rest a disjointed mess that wasted its notable supporting cast. Watch or Pass was kinder, recommending it as a rental for its intense opening, the crocodile ring, its imaginative locales and a comic undercover policeman fond of disguises, while finding the story hard to follow.

In Buffalo, Wyoming, in the late nineteenth century, McMasters is a widowed marshal with a reputation for bringing outlaws back dead, whose long absences have left his twelve-year-old son Chad resentful and in the care of his grandfather Dex. While Britt is away for three months tracking a bank robber and his accomplices, Jed Blake, an escaped prisoner whom McMasters once sent to jail for bank robbery, rides up to the ranch with his gang looking for revenge. Finding the marshal absent, Jed shoots Dex, leaving him badly wounded on the porch, kills Chad's young friend Albert and kidnaps Chad, knowing that his father will follow. When Britt returns and learns what has happened, Sheriff Wilkins, a longtime friend, cannot join the pursuit and assigns his inexperienced deputy Clay Tucker to accompany him. Because Tucker lacks tracking skills, they enlist Chaska, a Pawnee tracker with a white missionary mother, whom the racist deputy refuses to trust. Hot on the gang's trail, the small posse follows Jed into the Red Desert and into Sioux territory, where war parties have left dead settlers in their wake, while Chad tries to escape his captors and Jed prepares to settle his old score with the marshal.

The film was released in select US cinemas and on digital platforms on 10 September 2021, and on DVD and Blu-ray days later. Reviews were mostly negative. Mark Franklin of Once Upon a Time in a Western found it not bad for a modern Western, praising the gritty performances of Pickett and Gattlin Griffith. Jim Morazzini of Nerdly gave it 2.5 out of 5, calling it predictable and flatly directed, and noting that Skerritt and Facinelli had little screen time. Carla Hay of Culture Mix dismissed it as an amateurish dud with cringeworthy dialogue.

The story is set in a dystopian Europe where most of the population has been wiped out by a deadly virus. John Wood (Stisen), a special forces soldier who is immune to the disease, deserts his armed unit after its commander, Stone (Nehme), takes him captive and murders his wife; Stone is convinced that controlling a cure will hand him an empire. Years later Wood lives as a brooding hermit in a cabin in the Nordic wilderness, spending his days chopping wood, until a badly wounded woman, Maria (Kent), stumbles out of the forest one night. She has escaped from a laboratory, and her pursuers believe her blood holds the key to a worldwide cure. Wood reluctantly nurses her back to health and slowly grows used to her company, but armed soldiers soon track them to the cabin and launch a series of deadly attacks. When he learns that the man hunting Maria is Stone, Wood casts aside his doubts and prepares for a final confrontation.

Critics noted the film's deliberate homage to 1980s muscle-bound action films. Birger Vestmo of NRK's Filmpolitiet gave it three out of six, describing it as an old-fashioned actioner of the kind once rented on VHS, plainly modelled on Commando, with the same awkward one-liners but plenty of cheerful violent drive, and judged that Stisen proved capable of far more than his earlier extra work. Lee B. Golden III of Film Combat Syndicate saw potential in Stisen but found much of the fight work more miss than hit, the timeline confusing and the villain's backstory a contrived twist. Emilie Black of Cinema Crazed praised a few well-executed fights but felt the familiar story lost the viewer's interest early and much of the acting was wooden.

Lacey Samon (Field) heads to a beach rental house for a week by the sea with her two teenage children, played by Hargrave and Grogan, continuing a family tradition begun by her father Noah (Lauer), an ailing man who relies on an oxygen tank and joins them on the trip. Her husband (Lawrence) is supposed to follow by car from San Francisco. On arrival the family discovers that badly needed repairs on the house were never finished, leaving the basement flooded just as a powerful storm rolls in. What begins as a relaxing getaway turns into a nightmare when the rising floodwater carries a hungry shark into the house. Trapped by the storm, with the water climbing and injuries slowing them down, the family must fend off the predator inside the flooded rooms, improvising weapons from household objects while trying to stay above the waterline. Noah makes a sacrifice to protect the others, and the father finally arrives late in the film to join the fight for survival.

Swim premiered on the free streaming service Tubi on 13 August 2021. Much of it was filmed in a pool and on built sets, and it was shot in a widescreen 2.39:1 format that gave it a slightly more polished look than many comparable low-budget productions. Reviews were largely negative. Knockout Horror gave it one and a half stars out of five, acknowledging the cast's commitment under waterlogged shooting conditions and the film's relatively expensive appearance but criticizing its thin script, implausible casting of family members' ages, shark effects that kept changing scale, poor lighting and visible continuity errors. Cinematic Diversions was more forgiving, rating it six out of ten as an entertaining if clumsy entry in the genre, with decent shark effects and a story that was serviceable by the standards of shark movies, though it mocked the late appearance of top-billed Lawrence.

In fictional Yunjiang county in south-west China, a construction team is completing a tunnel through Yundang mountain for a high-speed railway after ten years of work, in a region of fragile karst rock destabilised by movement of the Indian Ocean plate. When a blast supervised by the young engineer Hong Yizhou (Zhu) floods the tunnel, he and his girlfriend, the radar technician Lu Xiaojin (Jiao), divert the water into a cavern, and project manager Ding Yajun (Chen) halts work, although her superiors insist the line must open on time. Abseiling down the mountain to place sensors, Yizhou finds abnormal rock activity. Meanwhile his gruff father, the retired railway soldier Hong Yunbing (Huang), arrives in town just as an earthquake strikes and a vast sinkhole swallows his coach. After helping rescue survivors, Yunbing disappears underground, where he leads a small group of survivors, including a stowaway boy, through the caves. Yizhou races to find him and takes over the group, but old tensions between father and son resurface. Ding plans to blast away part of the mountain to stop it collapsing onto the rail bridge, but the predicted landslide shifts towards Yunjiang, a town of 160,000 that cannot be evacuated in time, as a storm approaches. To save the town, the railway builders resolve to blow up the tunnel that cost them a decade of work; Yizhou proves himself to his father, overcoming a phobia from his youth, and a great sacrifice is made along the way.

After a Chinese warship enters American waters while relaying classified US government information to a satellite, it is attacked and sunk by a megalodon. Nearby, an American warship commanded by Lynch is on patrol; Lynch is troubled because her sister faces a court-martial for allegedly sinking her own ship on purpose, and her claim that a giant shark was responsible has been dismissed as a lie. The crew recovers Dr. Lee, a scientist who survived the sinking in a life raft, and another Chinese warship under Captain Ping demands her return, threatening to treat a refusal as an act of war, with the crewmember Tuan acting as interpreter.

Tensions rise when three megalodons attack the Chinese ship and then the American vessel, leading Ping to suspect the Americans can control the sharks. When gunner Samperio kills one of the creatures, the others feed on it, allowing the ships to escape. Lynch contacts Moore, and the sharks head for a crowded beach in San Diego, where troops are sent to defend the coast; Dr. Lee and the radio operator Wilco lure them away by imitating the satellite signal. Returning to sea, the sharks sink the Chinese reinforcements one by one. The Americans rescue the Chinese survivors, kill a second shark with their guns, and Lynch makes peace with Ping before the two crews kill the last one together, although Wilco dies. Lynch publicly announces the attacks and the new alliance with China, but a final sonar reading reveals two more objects in the ocean.

Because of COVID-19 restrictions, the film used very few extras, and the sharks and many warship shots were created with CGI. German critics dismissed its effects, dialogue and characters, finding little to recommend beyond the sharks themselves.

The film opens with a half-glimpsed furry creature killing a drunken fisherman on a lake under the full moon. When he fails to come home, his wife Sarah (Cole) reports him missing, one of several disappearances troubling the small town. Police chief Galligan (Repas) sends Detective Ryan Conner (Hillis), a tough, conservative military veteran haunted by memories of his wartime service, to investigate with his partner Dave (Migra), the chief's son. Meanwhile, at Talbot's Wolf Sanctuary, Maggie Talbot (Westwood) marks the first anniversary of her parents' deaths while trying, with the help of Todd (Guerrero), to keep their dream alive. When a mutilated body is found in the forest after a mysterious animal attack, Conner is forced to enlist the eager wildlife specialist to help him uncover the dark truth threatening the town. Flashbacks to Conner's combat experience punctuate the investigation, and the hunt ends with a twist revealing the identity of the creature.

The film drew mixed reviews. Jim Morazzini, writing for Voices From the Balcony in a review republished by Nerdly, gave it two and a half stars out of five, finding it badly flawed but watchable; he praised the use of a practical man-in-a-suit creature rather than CGI but felt the heavy subplot about post-traumatic stress disorder would alienate viewers expecting a werewolf film, and called the final reveal, which hinges on a character never established as a suspect, a lazy cheat. Jeff Turner of Action Reloaded was more enthusiastic, calling it a howling good time with solid performances from Hillis and Westwood, intriguing backstories, a gruesome war flashback and an effective practical-effects creature, and noting that the ending left the door open for a sequel.

Princess Amelia (Patterson), the polished royal of a fictional European kingdom, is due to fly home after a speaking engagement on the East Coast of the United States when mechanical problems ground her plane. While the crew is busy with the repairs and an old-fashioned snowstorm settles over the area, she slips away from the aircraft to wander through a magical Christmas tree lot near the edge of the airport. Through a series of mishaps she ends up stranded in Tucker, a small, snow-covered seaside town in Maine full of quaint scenery and Christmas lights. There she is taken in as an ordinary guest by the unsuspecting Cutler family, including widower Sam Cutler (Donovan) and his young daughter Sophie (Boyle), who do not know who she really is. As Amelia experiences small-town holiday traditions with them, she and Sam grow close and each learns lessons that leave them with renewed hope, while she must decide when to reveal her royal identity.

Reviews from holiday-film critics were mixed. Rissi JC of RissiWrites called it a sweet happenstance romance whose derivative plot mattered little given its cute story and its likable, familiar leads; she found the production less polished than its competitors, with busy backgrounds and some awkward transitions, but praised the script for letting the revelation of Amelia's secret unfold without the usual dramatic fallout. The Terrible Christmas Movie Project was harsher, judging the chemistry and plot merely fine and the film boring, and mocking Patterson's vaguely British accent, which it said slipped away in most scenes. The Christmas Everyday Club found it cute, festive and at times funny, with two leads who worked well together.

Set in and around a small, snowbound town, the film follows two modest couples who are drawn into a deadly game with a vicious gang after a mysterious box buried long ago comes to light. A prologue set in the frontier past shows a horseback pursuit through wintry woods that ends with an execution and the killer taking the box. More than a century later, a man burying his dog, which has been mauled to death, unearths the well-preserved wooden box, and his decision to have a coin from it appraised sets a chain of killers on him, his wife and anyone thought to know where the box is. A thug, played by Biskupek, and his girlfriend handle the box, his nephew Joel, played by Canning, who has a pregnant partner, asks to join the gang's work, and the gang's enforcers torture suspects in their search. One captive, Wade, played by Swatton, is taken into the woods and shot but survives, and after returning home to find his wife dead he sets out for vengeance. Meanwhile a near-silent detective, Bronwyn, played by Meyer, arrives at crime scenes after the fact and tries to piece together who is responsible. The contents of the box are never revealed, and the timeline shifts back and forth with little dialogue to guide the viewer.

The film was released in North America by Blue Fox Entertainment in March 2022, and High Fliers Films scheduled a UK release for October 2022. Reviews were largely negative. Roger Moore of Movie Nation called it a muddled, incoherent thriller driven by greed rather than revenge, faulting its jumping timeline and uneven acting. The Rotting Zombie, comparing its snowy setting to Fargo, found it a glacial and almost dialogue-free experiment that still managed to tell its story, singling out Biskupek's performance but felt its subplots amounted to little and that its pace would deter many viewers.

The film opens with a poor man being arrested in a slum as his children watch in tears. Years later, Chief Inspector Harun (Erdoğan) is named police officer of the year for his work against Istanbul's murders, with a further promotion apparently imminent. After celebrating with his team, he takes a taxi home and dozes off, only to wake in a remote wooded area where the driver tries to kill him. Harun kills his attacker in the struggle but, instead of reporting it, wipes the scene and tells no one. The next morning the cabbie's body is found hanging from a construction crane in full view of police headquarters, and Harun's young protégé Tuncay (Üzümoğlu) quietly finds and hides the tie clip that colleagues had given Harun the night before. As his team, including his lieutenant Yadigar (Aksoy), investigates, Harun runs his own frantic inquiry, threatening old informants and accidentally killing a key witness in a shootout, and he uncovers links between the cabbie and the deaths of three fellow officers. A mysterious woman, Gülendam (Sarışın), then confesses to the killings and reveals to Harun that she is the daughter of a man wrongly arrested years earlier for a mass murder who later died; to avenge him she is killing the officers involved, and she asks Harun to kill his boss Cevat (Taylan). Released as a fantasist, she kills Cevat herself and, before taking her own life, reveals that her brother is Tuncay. After killing Yadigar, Tuncay confesses that he himself committed the poisonings for which their father was blamed, and kills himself. Exposed for the cabbie's death, Harun is led away in handcuffs before his son Aslan, completing Tuncay's revenge.

Reviews were mixed. Jade Budowski of Decider praised Erdoğan, a standout Sarışın and the tight script, while Roger Moore of Movie Nation found it decently plotted but hampered by obvious foreshadowing and a cautious ending.

Apparently set in the 1930s, the story follows a young Ip Man, a gifted fighter who arrives in the big city for the first time with no idea of the corruption he will face. When he stops a kidnapping, he stumbles upon a large-scale human trafficking ring run by arrogant British colonialists led by Mr. Stark, who round up local women with the help of police officers on the take and Chinese collaborators more interested in money than in their compatriots. His intervention ignites a turf war with the gang. In retaliation, the traffickers kidnap one of Ip Man's close friends, and after suffering losses and setbacks, he sets out to rescue the captive women, defend Chinese pride against the colonial bullies and confront the group's brutal boxing champion and finally Stark himself.

Distributed in North America by Well Go USA, the film premiered on the Hi-Yah! streaming service on 20 May 2022 and was later released on Blu-ray; in the United Kingdom it reached the Icon Film Channel in April 2023 and cinemas in May. Reviews were mixed. Mark Glass of We Are Movie Geeks gave it three out of four stars, calling Tse a worthy successor in the role and a likely rising star, and noting that although the early fights suffered from close camerawork and choppy editing, the later ones were polished. He also highlighted the novelty of bartitsu. Phil Hoad of The Guardian was harsher, describing it as a clunky attempt to cash in on Yen's superior series with a laughably thin narrative and pantomime villains who speak oddly accented English, though he found Tse spry and convincing in the generally competent fight scenes.

Jessica Roberts (Lawson) runs the most popular Christmas tree lot in Hudson Springs, a picturesque small town in New England, on her family's farm. Clay Moore (Russell), a big-city marketing executive, arrives to open a big-box store whose tree sales threaten local family businesses, and above all Jessica's. The two meet and are immediately attracted to each other before either realises who the other is. Once Jessica learns Clay's true identity, she turns against him and sets out to beat him at his own game, but the escalating competition is complicated by their growing feelings for each other. Her efforts to outdo the store prove costly, and her younger brother Scott (Visser) eventually has to tell her that the lot's expenses have outstripped its sales and pushed the business to the brink. A sudden idea to turn the farm into an event venue offers a way to save it, while Clay, discovering that the corporation he works for has been built on lies, decides that small-town life suits him better, clearing the way for the romance.

Reception was limited and mixed. Writing on the blog Rebekah's Readings and Watchings, the reviewer rated the film six out of ten, saying that Russell, cast against his usual type of rugged outdoorsman as a corporate executive, was excellent, funny and sincere, and that Lawson was fine, though her character came across as trying too hard and her escalating antics made her less sympathetic than the good-natured Clay. The review found the story dull and the farm's rescue implausibly quick, and admitted that Russell was the main reason for finishing the film.

Ally Morgan is a dedicated emergency room doctor whose long night shifts leave little room for her relationship with her boyfriend Josh. When she is promoted to an administrative post, Josh hopes they will finally have more time together, but Ally cannot bring herself to leave the ER behind, and his patience with her work-life balance runs out until he ends the relationship. Miserable on her own and in no mood for Christmas, Ally has a chance encounter with Gabe, a handsome and mysterious barista, who leads her through a Christmas bucket list of festive activities she would never have tried alone, helping her learn to switch off and make room for herself. Her best friend and fellow ER doctor Dawn has never seen Ally so engaged outside work and roots for a romance between her and Gabe. Gabe, however, is an angel, and as he and Ally grow too close, the saintly Maureen must redirect his heartfelt intentions so that Josh and Ally have a chance at reconciliation before Christmas.

The film premiered on GAC Family on 26 November 2021 and later reached Netflix in Germany in December 2022. Critical response was mixed to negative. The Terrible Christmas Movie Project called it weird, boring and confusing, objecting to a story in which the heroine spends the film growing close to one man before returning to the boyfriend who left her, and finding Murray's slow, over-enunciated delivery as the angel highly distracting. Paul Siwasch of Film-Rezensionen.de was more forgiving, describing it as unremarkable and safely conventional but calm, with small twists, solid acting and a heartwarming angel-themed premise that made it acceptable viewing for a December afternoon, though he criticised the cheap-looking setting and the German dubbing of Murray.

Jamie (Garth) runs a successful sightseeing and tour company in the small town of Cooperville, New York, and knows better than anyone where to find fun things to do. Since the death of her husband Matt, who adored Christmas and found his greatest joy in giving to others, facing the holidays with the same enthusiasm has been harder for her. With the support of her niece, a newlywed who is more like a younger sister to her, she tries to keep up a brave front. Jamie is a devoted viewer of the morning programme Wake Up Upstate and has a crush on its handsome anchor, Scott Morris (Mathison). When the show reports that students from a neighbouring high school have been invited to perform at the White House but cannot afford the trip, Jamie, remembering Matt's belief that Christmas is about bringing joy to others, anonymously covers the entire cost. Her gift inspires another and then another, until the whole town catches the spirit of giving. The mystery of Cooperville's Secret Santa draws Scott to town to uncover the donor's identity, and after some awkward first encounters with Jamie, a romance develops between them, tested when the truth about her secret comes out.

Reviews were positive about the leads. Markos Papadatos of Digital Journal gave the film an A, praising Leite-Rogers's direction, a heartfelt and resonant screenplay and the delightful performances of Garth and Mathison, describing Mathison's acting as subtle and poignant. OTTplay's reviewer called it formulaic but heartwarming, enjoying the Secret Santa premise and the adorable chemistry between Jamie and Scott, whose slow-building romance was found engaging, though Mathison's character seemed out of place when he storms off during the couple's late conflict; the review concluded that the endearing cast and its message about the joy of giving made it a touching holiday story.

Yusuf, a successful criminal lawyer, has not seen his father since the day after his mother's funeral, some twenty-five years earlier. Heves Ali, a well-known travelling musician and wandering bard, turns up unexpectedly at his door after visiting his late wife's grave and, kept there by heavy rain, stays the night, explaining only that he must travel to Kars for the troubadour festival. When Yusuf discovers that the old man's health is failing and that his visit is a kind of farewell, he feels responsible for him and decides to drive him there himself. Much of the long road trip across the Turkish countryside passes in uneasy silence, broken by stops at places the father chooses on a whim, as he seeks out old musician friends and asks forgiveness of former lovers he once serenaded. Yusuf's years of anger eventually erupt, and he demands to know why he was abandoned, but his father offers little beyond saying he felt his son was better off without him. As Ali's condition worsens he is taken to hospital, yet he insists on reaching the festival, and Yusuf takes him to Kars in a private ambulance to fulfil his wish of seeing his friends one last time, leaving their relationship unresolved.

Critics praised the performances and the role of music and silence. Mrinal Rajaram of Cinema Express gave it three out of five, calling it a brooding, character-driven study of a dysfunctional father-son bond whose pauses and folk songs say more than its sparse dialogue. The Review Geek rated it 7 out of 10, admiring its cinematography and Tanrıöğen's weary performance but finding it slow and overstretched. Shraddha Bandapalle of The Envoy singled out Tatlıtuğ's portrayal of a son's rage and grief, while noting that the leisurely, non-linear storytelling sometimes left the film feeling static.

Whitney Alder (Wagner) owns the interior design firm Marietta Designs, which she runs with her friend Andi (Moss) in the small town of Marietta, Montana. While she is designing Santa's float for the town's annual Christmas parade, a tempting opportunity arrives: the complete redesign of a landmark home, to be finished by Christmas Eve. Despite the tight deadline, Whitney and Andi take the job, only to discover that the house's new owner is Whitney's former boyfriend, Connor Sheenan (Bateman), who has moved to Marietta from Los Angeles with his bright-eyed young daughter, Daisy (Tupper). Connor never intended to become a family man, but when his goddaughter was orphaned he adopted her and committed himself to being a devoted single father. Working together in the house brings back a trove of forgotten memories for Whitney and Connor, while Daisy, whose greatest wish is for a mother to complete her family, decides that Whitney is the perfect candidate, leaving it to the season of miracles to bring the former couple a second chance.

Reviews from holiday-film writers were generally warm. Rissi JC of RissiWrites found the film charming, sweet and better than expected, with a fun spin on a familiar trope; she noted that its production values were not quite equal to those of rival networks and praised Wagner while being less convinced by her co-star. Christiana of My Movie Views gave it 7.5 out of 10, calling it an ordinary but enjoyable Christmas film. In Porter's novel the hero is media mogul Cormac Sheenan, and four-year-old Daisy befriends Marietta's seasonal Santa Claus, whom she believes to be the real one.

Don Servando, known to the family as the grumpy grandfather, has become part of a larger and more unconventional household since the events of the first film: besides Fran and Alma, it includes a carefree commune of fun-loving hippies such as Gala, Renato and Bill. This year the whole group sets off on a trip to the beach to spend the holidays with Doña Alicia, a stubborn and demanding woman who quickly becomes Servando's ultimate nemesis. The two elders clash over how Christmas should be celebrated and over who really rules the family. Feeling that his position as patriarch is under threat, Servando stops at nothing to prove to everyone that Alicia is a terrible, self-centered person, even if it means ruining the holiday for all of them. Around their feud, the film weaves a series of smaller subplots involving the other relatives, and the sunny seaside setting replaces the usual snowy holiday backdrop, though snow does eventually make an appearance before the family rediscovers the spirit of unity.

Grumpy Christmas was released on Netflix on 21 December 2021, and was presented in Brazil as Natal, mas Pouco. Reviews were lukewarm.
