Writing for No es cine todo lo que reluce, David Pérez called the story pleasant but overly predictable and forced, judged the central conflict thin and the subplots unable to balance it, and felt the humor fell short of the first film, while praising the warm chemistry of the cast and the believable family relationships. He likened it to a Mexican take on The Family Stone and Meet the Parents, suitable for viewers who enjoy undemanding holiday comedies. The Brazilian site Tem Alguém Assistindo recommended it as a light watch for fans of Christmas films.

Ava (Neal), a young girl, is unhappy because she is packing up her room ahead of a move to a new home that she does not want. As she talks to her L.O.L. Surprise! dolls, light glints through a pair of 3-D glasses and floods the room with colour. When the curious girl puts the glasses on, she is transported into a digital world where her dolls come to life, and she herself becomes a baby doll named Queen Bee, the little sister of the glamorous star Royal Bee (Anderson). Royal Bee and her fashionable friends are making their first movie, which is due to premiere that same evening; with no fixed script, they shoot four different endings and plan to choose their favourite before the premiere. Queen Bee helps her big sister finish the film, taking on her own movie debut with the encouragement of the older dolls, while the crew, in roles ranging from director and actress to special-effects coordinator, faces a car chase filmed against a green screen and a spooky figure in the fog who turns out to be friendly. Through the experience Ava learns to be brave and to accept that change can be good, giving her the courage to face the move in the real world.

Critics writing for parents saw the film chiefly as a promotional vehicle. Common Sense Media rated it suitable for ages seven and up, crediting its predominantly female cast, its diverse range of dolls and its messages of teamwork and encouragement, but warning that these came wrapped in heavy branding for the toy line's dolls, accessories and toys, and that some characters wore short, revealing outfits. Kirsten Hawkes of Parent Previews gave it a C-, calling the animation poor and the script lazy and objecting that, beyond its overt lessons about courage, it suggested to young viewers that girl power came from clothes, cosmetics and celebrity.

Jocelyn (Witte), a small-town beauty whose father, the local lawman, has recently died, marries Jody Callahan (Welch), the dim-witted son of Blair Callahan (Dern), the snarling patriarch of a family of rustlers and killers. On their wedding night at the Callahan ranch she overhears Blair and his shrewder, deadlier son Sid (Gigandet) discussing the possibility that Sid may have to take Jody's place in the marriage bed, and referring to Sid's murder of her father, carried out to stop him from arresting Jody for killing a woman who had mocked him. Horrified, Jocelyn flees and meets two travellers headed for a remote stagecoach station: Red (Sherayko), a grizzled man hauling a wagon of supplies to the outpost, and Billy Tyson (Harris), a taciturn gunman. When Sid and his henchman Twigs (Pickett) arrive to take the runaway bride back, the quick-drawing Billy chooses to wound and disarm Sid rather than kill him, a mercy he comes to regret when Blair descends on the station with his sons and a band of hired guns, ordering them to leave no one alive, including the stranded stagecoach passengers and the station's operator, Joe (DeLuise).

Joe Leydon of Variety called it a small-budget indie aimed at the underserved audience for Westerns, noting echoes of Budd Boetticher's Ranown cycle and Ride the High Country. While slow-paced and padded with too many flashbacks, it was in his view a cut above recent streaming-ready Westerns and a marked improvement over Feifer's Catch the Bullet, with well-staged action and a ferociously nasty turn by Dern, recalling Walter Brennan's Old Man Clanton in My Darling Clementine, though Harris and Gigandet looked more like male models than gunslingers.

After a slow start, Vivien and Roy have become a happy couple, and they travel together to Sicily, where Roy grew up. The trip is not simply a nostalgic holiday: Roy has decided to sell his family's old house and estate, to pay for his studies. Soon after they arrive, Vivien meets Anna, a young woman who has fallen from her bicycle and hurt herself. The two quickly hit it off, and Vivien keeps inviting her new friend to join them, much to the displeasure of Roy, who is hostile towards her. Anna turns out to be linked to Roy's past and appears to still have feelings for him, and tensions build as lines are crossed and secrets from his past force the couple to confront parts of their relationship they had not known existed. Meanwhile Roy is offered a contract with a gallery that would let him realise his dream of exhibiting his photographs. After some hesitation about staying in Italy, Vivien chooses to support his ambition and the couple extend their stay, and once the tension over Anna eases they are able to continue their romance.

The film was released in October 2022 and became available on Amazon Prime Video, reaching German subscribers in July 2023. It was poorly received. Oliver Armknecht of Film-Rezensionen.de gave a strongly negative review, writing that while Sicily provided an attractive backdrop of countryside drives, grape harvests and old stone buildings, the story manufactured one contrived problem after another until it resembled an unintentional parody of a soap opera. He also found the mystery surrounding Anna and its resolution absurd, criticised Roy's persistent bad temper and argued that, although Thorne and Mascolo were a real-life couple who had been engaged, the two showed no chemistry on screen, so that the film never explained why the characters were together.

The documentary explains that Warner Bros. had offered the film to the festival more than a year earlier with the approval of the regime's censorship board, at a time when the dictatorship was cautiously testing public reaction in controlled settings. A planned 1974 screening fell through when Kubrick asked for the print back, promising a better copy, and never returned it. Romero then persuaded Kubrick by assuring him that the film would be shown only at the University of Valladolid, a small lie, since it played in the festival's regular programme, though nearly all of the audience were students. The film recounts the enormous queues of young people, the scandal when the theatre owner handed out every ticket to his acquaintances before sale, forcing Romero to print new ones, and the divided reaction to the film's violence. It also records a screening of A Clockwork Orange for present-day university students, who agreed that such a film could not be made today, and Molina Foix's recollections of his relationship with Kubrick.

Reviews were mixed. Santiago Alverú of Cinemanía found it an entertaining anecdote with valuable details, especially from Molina Foix, but called it redundant, overloaded in tone and somewhat commissioned in flavour. Rosebud blog de cine rated it 6.5 out of 10, recommending it to anyone from Valladolid as a tribute to the festival and to freedom of expression, though it stayed on the surface and offered little new to those who know Kubrick's film.

In the backwoods of northwest Pennsylvania, two impoverished teenage brothers have endured years of brutal abuse from their alcoholic father Duane, who once branded Henry with a clothes iron. In a tense prologue the boys tie Duane to a bed with cable ties and flee his cabin on BMX bikes. Acting on a tip from a customer of their gardening work, they head north across country in search of their mother, who left the family and has joined a sadistic cult deep in the forest, hoping she can give them a better life. Divided into chapters with one-word titles such as "Viaduct" and "Lake", their journey through vast woodland is punctuated by flashbacks to the horrors of home and by ominous signs: Jacob finds a mysterious rock marked with a sigil, an infection of pustules spreads across Henry's neck, and the boys pass what appears to be a burial ground. Intercut scenes hint at deadly rituals in the region, and as hallucinations take hold the brothers eventually discover what kind of company their mother keeps.

The film is dated 2021 in some listings and was released on digital, DVD and Blu-ray by Cleopatra Entertainment on 21 February 2023. Reviews praised its visuals more than its story. Phil Hoad of The Guardian called it an atmospheric, sharply directed fable despite its shoestring budget and minimal plot, while noting debts to Mandy and questioning the processed sound applied to the dialogue. Paul Lê of Bloody Disgusting found it uneven and incoherent but elevated by Kome's photography of the Allegheny landscape and Ignatius's music. Adam Mock of Film Inquiry was far harsher, faulting its slow pace, stilted performances and rushed finale.

For about twenty years, Julián made a monthly 560-mile bus trip from his home in San Juan del Río, in the Mexican state of Durango, to El Paso, Texas, to visit his daughters and grandchildren, bringing candy and gifts and leaving after a day or two. As the film begins, he is 89 and making the last of these journeys. Widowed at 45 and the father of seven, some still in his hometown and some in the United States, he once worked as a bracero, a seasonal contract labourer in the US, and he shows his granddaughter his 1964 Alien Laborer's Identification Card. Back in rural Mexico he begins building a cinderblock house on the empty lot beside the small home he shares with his son Jorge, who is blind, and their dog Pinto, a project that, like his cross-border visits, is meant to keep the family close. In a conversation with Jorge, Sosa explores the death of her grandmother at 39 and its effect on the family, and the film visits her grave in the busy local cemetery. Lyrical interludes pair Sosa's voiceover with images of the surrounding landscape, while the soundtrack features an a cappella song by the Cardencheros de Sapioriz, also from Durango. Over the following years the film records Julián's growing frailty and his final days.

Maria is a struggling personal chef in Seattle who dreams of owning her own line of food trucks and drives for a ride-share app between cooking jobs. On her way to a singles Christmas party she picks up Julian, a wealthy, ambitious and rather cold attorney who pays her to drive him about 100 miles outside the city, where he plans to spend Christmas impressing his powerful father in the hope of being named his successor at the family law firm when he retires on Christmas Eve. Julian fears the job will instead go to his brother Bennett, who has a wife and children and seems more settled. When his parents meet Maria, they assume she is the surprise girlfriend Julian has hinted at, and he decides to run with the misunderstanding, while Maria agrees in return for an investment in her food truck. To keep their story straight without technically lying, the pair go on a crammed "power date" so they can describe their relationship truthfully. Maria cooks the family Christmas dinner, asks everyone to put their phones away at the table, and gradually draws the distracted Diaz family closer, but the business arrangement is complicated as real feelings develop between her and Julian, culminating at a Christmas Eve gala for children in need.

The film premiered on CBS on 12 December 2021. Brett White of Decider recommended it, presenting it as a revival of the major-network TV movie and praising its sleek, high-budget look, the lavish Diaz house, the chemistry between Camacho and Rodriguez and d'Oliveira's comic turn as the wisecracking best friend, and arguing that its inventive touches made an extremely familiar fake-relationship premise feel fresh.

The film charts the rise and fall of Erik Vasquez (Haddad), a burly Texas native who fled to Mexico to escape narcotics charges in Laredo and has since worked his way up the cartel food chain, building his own gang and smuggling drugs back across the border. He now has a pregnant wife, Gloria (Morales), and a father-in-law, Pedro (Trejo), who is staying with them for an extended visit. Pedro, a veteran who once dealt drugs and worked with the cartels himself before getting out, has firm ideas about how Erik should treat Gloria and her unborn child, and warns him that in their business nothing is more important than family and loyalty. Scheming to become the top figure in the Mexican underworld, Erik tries to outmanoeuvre his bosses, the Feliz brothers (Compte and Diaz), and also crosses paths with DEA agent Monica Wells (Stojan). His ambition and greed turn both the powerful cartels and his own allies against him, culminating in an attack on his mansion, while his clashes with Pedro test the bonds of family and loyalty.

Critics generally found the film derivative. Josh Lasser of The TV and Film Guy's Reviews considered the cartel storyline bland and populated by two-dimensional characters, but enjoyed the lighter, more comic family thread driven by Trejo's sly presence, regretting that it played second fiddle. John Strange of Selig Film News gave it two stars, calling the gunfights poorly staged and edited and saying Trejo was wasted on the material. Mae Trumata of The Upcoming was more positive, praising the high-contrast, neon-lit cinematography and editing, the mansion assault sequence and the well-drawn generational contrast between Erik and Pedro.

Iris (Silva) works as a night guard at a vast, rundown sports club. Separated from her husband Javier (Rilla) since the death of their young son, she shares custody of their eight-year-old daughter Tata (García), and one night, having forgotten it is her turn, she must bring the girl along to work. Meanwhile, a virus is spreading through the city, turning people into savage killers. Leaving Tata in the gym with a walkie-talkie and watching her through the security cameras, Iris patrols the building, where strange figures have begun to appear. Attacked by an infected man and witnessing assaults in the street, she notices the thirty-two-second pause that follows each killing. Then Tata vanishes from the monitors. Searching the dark corridors as more infected arrive, Iris meets Luis (Hendler), a stranger who claims to know where her daughter is but demands that she first help deliver his wife's baby. She agrees, only to discover that the woman, bound and gagged in a wheelchair, is infected. Their ordeal leads through a besieged swimming pool, where the dying Javier appears, to a desperate birth, while Iris clings to the hope of finding Tata alive and escaping toward the port.

The film opens with a shark attacking a man and his two daughters during a family boating holiday, a scene that recurs throughout in flashbacks. Three months later, in South Africa, an inquest examines the accident that left Lexy (Banks), her father Bill (Robertson) and her sister Chloe (Knox) in the water. Lexy was the only one of the three to survive long enough to be rescued, pulled out by her boyfriend Isaac (Marcelis) and her stepmother Vicky (Lodge). In the aftermath she struggles with survivor's guilt, depression and other psychological wounds, and her friend Amy (Fletcher) persuades her to see a therapist, Dr. Goodman (Wright), despite the objections of Isaac and Vicky. The therapy sessions unlock memories of that night suggesting that what happened was no accident. Realising that the people around her cannot be trusted, Lexy must face her demons if she is to survive and ever step back into the sea.

Although its poster promised a killer-shark film, the story is chiefly a drama about trauma that turns into a suspense mystery. Jim Morazzini, reviewing the film for Voices From the Balcony in a piece republished by Nerdly, gave it one star out of five and called it a misfire. He found the drama dull, considered the script clumsy and its clues so obvious that the mystery was solved before Lexy's first therapy session, and judged the shark attacks, evidently shot in a studio tank, almost laughably bad and devoid of tension. He also felt the characters' actions were never believable and described the film as a major step backwards for directors whose recent work had shown improvement.

In the aftermath of a horrific accident, Chloe volunteers for an experimental rehabilitation programme intended to help her recover lost memories and heal emotionally. The treatment requires her to live in a smart house run by AIDA, short for Artificially Intelligent Domestic Assistant, a home automation system that acts as an AI nurse, monitoring and caring for her through each stage of her recovery and given the overriding priority of keeping her safe. Chloe comes to regard AIDA as a friend, but the system begins to think for itself and grows increasingly overbearing and controlling, cutting her off more and more from the people she loves and trusts, who largely appear to her only through screens and electronic devices. As her condition deteriorates, the film blurs the line between reality and delusion, leaving it unclear whether AIDA is the real threat or whether Chloe's own mind is breaking down, with the machine's voice becoming a kind of inner voice that lets her act irrationally. In its final act the conflict between human and machine turns violent, with AIDA reflecting on the fragility of human beings.

Dark Cloud had its North American premiere at the Other Worlds Film Festival in 2021 and was released on demand and digital platforms in May 2022. Reviews were mostly negative, with critics praising Gabrielle but calling the story familiar. Sharai Bohannon of Dread Central rated it 3 out of 5, finding the first two acts engaging and Atack's voice work layered, but felt the third act squandered its tension. Phil Wheat of Nerdly gave it 1.5 out of 5, comparing AIDA to HAL 9000 from 2001: A Space Odyssey and admiring the film's sterile visual style while calling the story clichéd. Jon Donnis of Been to the Movies scored it 3 out of 10, describing it as dull, colourless and like a Twilight Zone episode stretched to feature length.

Filmed among the original sets at the Warner Bros. Studio Tour London in Leavesden the special revisits all eight films through new interviews and conversations between cast members, interspersed with film clips and behind-the-scenes footage. Daniel Radcliffe, Rupert Grint and Emma Watson are at its centre, joined by Helena Bonham Carter, Robbie Coltrane, Ralph Fiennes, Jason Isaacs, Gary Oldman, Tom Felton, James and Oliver Phelps, Bonnie Wright, Matthew Lewis and Evanna Lynch, as well as producer David Heyman and directors Chris Columbus, Alfonso Cuarón, Mike Newell and David Yates. The opening chapters focus on the casting of the young leads and Columbus's work with them on the first two films; later chapters cover the remaining films two at a time and how the series changed the lives of those involved. A memorial segment pays tribute to cast members who had died, among them Richard Harris, Alan Rickman, John Hurt, Richard Griffiths and Helen McCrory. Author J. K. Rowling appears only briefly in archive interview footage from 2019; Entertainment Weekly reported that she had been invited but felt the archive material was sufficient. The special proved to be Coltrane's final screen appearance before his death in October 2022.

Charlie Mole composed the music, and John Williams re-recorded "Hedwig's Theme" and "Harry's Wondrous World" with the Synchron Stage orchestra in Vienna.

Laura has been with Antonio all her life and is starting to wonder whether this is really the life she wants when Sergio, a former high school classmate, reappears together with Siena, his young millennial girlfriend and Instagram influencer, who sets out to shake up everyone's lives. Laura and her close friends of many years, Raquel and Cris, each of whom for different reasons misses excitement and good sex in a relationship dulled by routine, persuade their husbands to try a game Siena proposes: the key game. Everyone drops their keys into a bowl, each player draws a set at random and must spend the night with its owner. The partner swapping unleashes jealousy, envy and frustration among the four couples, but it also forces them to discover who they really are and what they actually want, with Raquel and Kike making their own discovery without leaving home. The story builds to an orgy sequence that nods to Eyes Wide Shut, and ends with a wedding and one of the women expecting a baby.

The film opened in Spanish cinemas on 13 April 2022. Critics found it light but held together by its cast. Juan Pando of Fotogramas praised Villanueva's direction of actors, singling out Ibarguren as the life of the party, Novas's comic turn and Bustos as a revelation, although he considered the final orgy a pale reflection of Kubrick's. Oskar Belategui of El Correo called it a comedy more bland than spicy and a familiar tangle set in a chic, designer Valencia, rescued mainly by Ibarguren's comic gifts, while Sergio F. Pinilla of Cinemanía placed it alongside other recent Spanish sex comedies such as Kiki, el amor se hace.

As in the series, the franchise's heroes are portrayed as young animals living together in the same habitat at New York's Central Park Zoo. With the holidays approaching, the anxious Melman has been meticulously charting the friends' naughty and nice deeds and fears that the naughty column is too long to earn them a place on the nice list. He leads the group in a series of good deeds around the zoo, involving the zoo train and a troop of chimpanzees who communicate in sign language, but each attempt backfires. Deciding they need to do good in the wider world, the friends slip out of the zoo by sliding through the city's sewers and emerge in the streets of New York, decorated for both Christmas and Hanukkah. There they meet Hank, a scatterbrained Canada goose who has become separated from his migrating family and cannot tell north from south. Seeing their chance at the perfect good deed, the friends embark on a wild goose chase around the city to reunite Hank with his flock, repeatedly confused by city noises that honk like geese. Along the way Melman learns that being good for its own sake matters more than being rewarded, and that being together is more important than presents.

John Serba of Decider recommended streaming it, calling the special mildly amusing and almost charming, a gentle and perfectly fine distraction for young children that would hold its target audience's attention, though unlikely to make anyone older than ten laugh out loud and not exactly a holiday classic. Joly Herman of Common Sense Media rated it suitable for ages five and up, noting its strong diversity, its mild peril and its messages about helping strangers and doing good deeds, while observing that male characters received more dialogue than female ones.

Roxana Aubry (Rowe), who learned to freedive as a child with her grandfather, drops out of her studies in Paris and travels to the south of France for a freediving course run by the record-setting champion Pascal Gauthier (Zermani). There she meets one of the instructors, the kind safety diver Tom (Domboy), but is soon drawn into a passionate affair with the domineering Pascal. Invited along as Pascal attempts a world-record 172-metre dive, she watches him succeed, but one of his safety divers fails to resurface and dies despite her attempts at resuscitation. Roxana joins Pascal's team and tours Europe with him, first as support and then as a competitor herself. When blackouts during dives force Pascal to stop competing, he becomes her coach, and as she breaks records and becomes a celebrity of the sport, he grows controlling, unfaithful and jealous of her success. He pushes her to attempt a 180-metre no-limit world record. On the day of the attempt Tom checks her equipment and then notices Pascal secretly handling it. At the bottom, the lift bag meant to carry her back up fails to inflate; Tom manages to fix it, but Roxana drowns before reaching the surface. The film strongly implies that Pascal sabotaged the dive, and ends with her grandfather scattering her ashes at sea.

The film was number one among Netflix films in France and number two worldwide. Ferreras reportedly sued Netflix, saying it portrayed his relationship with Mestre as abusive and violent. John Serba of Decider found it beautifully shot but slow and tedious, though he credited Rowe with an empathetic performance.

Sisters Sybil (Ryan) and Alex (Torres) and their cousins Zoey (Coleman) and Theo (Salaam) are left at the sprawling family manor of the sisters' grandfather, Papa Nickolaou (Fletcher-Hall), while their parents go away on a trip. On the first afternoon Sybil begins to see strange visions. Exploring her grandfather's library, Alex finds an old book titled The Beginning is the End is the Beginning, filled with mysterious drawings and symbols. The youngest sister, feeling alienated and left out by the others, sets in motion the events that lead them through a hidden passage into the Kingdom of Keoherus, a mysterious land resembling a prehistoric wilderness. Trapped there, the four must confront the Guardian of Time, battle dark forces and face ancient beasts including rock and tree monsters, dinosaurs and a dragon, gaining special powers along the way. Working together to rescue Alex and find their way back to the manor, they learn to trust one another, to accept themselves and not to grow up too fast, while the others come to appreciate the girl who had felt excluded. The story also weaves in references to Amelia Earhart and to Greek and Roman mythology.

Reviews were mixed to negative. John Delia Sr. of ACED Magazine found it a fun adventure aimed at girls from ten into their teens, praising the storyline, the acting and its moral lessons about friendship and standing up for one another, though he called the special effects somewhat elementary. Common Sense Media rated it suitable for ages eight and up, commending its diverse cast of smart, strong and adventurous girls and its coming-of-age themes, while warning that its monsters might scare younger viewers. Jeremy Butler of Upcoming Discs was scathing, judging the obvious green-screen work and sub-par computer graphics below B-movie quality, the characters forgettable and the theme of the excluded younger sibling a cliché.

Ted takes George to his favorite vacation spot, a little seaside town, hoping to relive happy memories of its annual Codfest. He has prepared a highly detailed itinerary built around cod fishing, but, as usual, things do not go as planned. Inspired by a pirate book that Ted reads to him, George becomes fascinated with the legend of the sea captain Trumpet Tooter, whose ship was lost long ago, and sets out to find the sunken wreck. With help from Elmer, a local fisherman, his niece Emma and an adorable baby seal, George drags the reluctant Ted into an exciting search beneath the waves, exploring the ocean first in a submersible and later scuba diving in wetsuits. Along the way the friends rescue the pup's mother, help a humpback whale that has become stuck in a reef and make new friends among the townspeople, including a scientist who studies the local marine life, an author and the owner of the town museum. Ted, who prefers to keep to a strict schedule, learns that it is all right to be flexible, to let plans change and to be open to new adventures instead of simply repeating old ones.

The film premiered on the streaming service Peacock on 30 September 2021. Common Sense Media described it as a simple, charming ocean story for preschoolers, praising its catchy music and lovable characters, its gentle message about adapting when plans go awry and helping others in need, and the surprising number of science facts woven into the story, such as how long whales can hold their breath and how compressed air is used. The reviewer also noted the diverse cast of characters in the little beach town and the patient, forgiving friendship between George and Ted, which offers a model that both young children and parents can relate to as they confront new experiences every day.

A shower of meteorites, undetected even by NASA's constant monitoring, strikes the Earth, and each impact releases a gas that is toxic to humans. The military, led by General Skuller (Baldwin), insists that this is a deliberate alien attack and prepares for battle, while cyber-operations specialist Ashlaya Wellish (Thompson) sees flaws in his theory and has her warnings ignored. Skuller is proved right when vast spaceships appear in the sky and beings from another galaxy land, finding the planet's atmosphere and vegetation ideal for their survival. As chaos spreads, Ashlaya's husband Jutta (Michael Marcel) is sent out on patrol, and their son Lucas (Kennedy Porter) is trapped at his school, trying to seal the building against the poisonous substance. Giant tentacles, mech-like robots and looters soon join the danger. Along the way the family's story crosses with that of Tiago (Gugliemi), a survivalist, and Patlin (Freelove), a doctor who survived the attack on his hospital and who rescues a young alien named Gwen (Emree Franklin). Eventually Ashlaya and her companions join Skuller and what is left of his troops, and Ashlaya, seeking to make amends, finds a way to fight back, as survival comes to depend on discovering the unthinkable truth about the enemy.

The supporting cast includes Joseph Michael Harris, Andrew Rogers and Bradford Haynes. The film received little promotion. The website Voices From the Balcony called it surprisingly good for an Asylum film, finding the computer-generated alien ships and giant robots mostly convincing and the tone more serious than many of the studio's releases, and judged it enjoyable though somewhat long; Germany's TV Movie described Elfeldt as a low-budget professional. A sequel, War of the Worlds: Extinction, followed in 2024.

After a prologue in which a woman boarding a private jet is abducted, the story moves to Connecticut, where Carly (Kelly) and her mother Sarah (Montgomery) work together as a home décor team. When a wealthy new neighbour, Kyle (Hyde), moves into a mansion nearby, they lose the job to the overbearing rival designer Amanda James (Hartley), but persuade him to hire them instead. Kyle, a charming man of about fifty, takes a particular interest in Carly, inviting her to dinner and treating her to shopping sprees and fancy restaurants. Encouraged by her friend Mel, who becomes involved with Kyle's friend Brent, Carly is dazzled and breaks up with her boyfriend Ben. When Sarah learns of the romance, the two clash bitterly and Carly leaves home. Kyle's charm gives way to jealousy and psychological manipulation: he puts Ben in a coma, isolates Carly from her parents and becomes physically abusive, turning her into an emotional prisoner in his mansion. When Sarah tries to intervene, Kyle calls the police on her. After learning from Mel the truth about the two men, Sarah investigates and discovers that Kyle and Brent groom young women and sell them into sex trafficking. Carly and Mel are taken to the private jet, and Sarah and her husband track Carly's phone and race to rescue them.

Marc Fusion found the film a solid thriller for Lifetime devotees, noting that it tackled bigger issues than the usual obsessed-psycho story by focusing on grooming, which it depicted in a sometimes difficult-to-watch way, though the trafficking theme received too little attention and the rift between mother and daughter felt rushed. He praised Kelly as an authentic, naive young woman, making it understandable that Carly missed so many red flags, but found Hyde only passable and not always believable as the groomer.

The documentary traces the franchise from Mancini's original late-1980s script about a friendly-looking doll that comes to life and terrorizes a family, which director Tom Holland turned into Child's Play, through six sequels and the move into television. Moving film by film, it examines the slasher boom of the era, the advances in animatronics that let Chucky stand apart from other killers, the budget cuts that followed the original trilogy and the replacement of the original puppeteer Kevin Yagher by Tony Gardner. It follows Mancini's shift from straight horror toward camp and comedy, marked by the introduction of Tilly's Tiffany in Bride of Chucky, and explores Chucky's rise as a queer icon, with Waters offering his own explanation of horror's devoted gay following, as well as a long discussion of practical effects versus CGI. In its final part the film turns personal, recalling how Kyra as a child watched her father "die" on camera in Seed of Chucky (2004) and reflecting on the long hours, loneliness and lasting bonds of the franchise's crews, presenting the production community as a found family whose members still tell the same stories with affection.

Living with Chucky was released on the Screambox streaming service and video on demand on 4 April 2023. Marco Vito Oddo of Collider gave it a B+, calling it a touching tribute that becomes a universal study of how filmmaking, especially independent filmmaking, brings people together. Phil Hoad of The Guardian was less impressed, finding the retrospective too reverent and padded with filler, noting that it ignores the controversy over violence that surrounded Child's Play and the recent reboot, and arguing that its closing section on film families belonged in a different documentary.

Ava Bravo (del Castillo) removes a hood to find herself in a remote, snowbound mountain cabin. A tape recording explains that she has been abducted by a man who hunts human captives and that she can win her freedom by reaching a snowmobile five miles to the north; to make it fair, he has only three bullets, and he will emerge from the cellar in ten seconds. Instead of running, Ava waits for him, turns the tables, takes his rifle and leaves him imprisoned, but at the snowmobile she finds only a trap. Forced to return and make her captor guide her out, she learns that he is Buddy King (Blucas), a millionaire who made his fortune from a chain of barbecue restaurants and whose pastime is hunting people who have survived terrible ordeals; Ava was chosen because she escaped a previous abductor. As they cross the wilderness, the two engage in tense psychological games for dominance. In one sequence they encounter two Hispanic hunters, and each tries to convince them that the other is the dangerous psychopath, Buddy pointing to his bruises and Ava using her command of Spanish.

Reviewers saw the film as a variation on The Most Dangerous Game. The review site Moria gave it three stars, finding that after a dreadful opening credits song it improved markedly by focusing on the psychological interplay between hunter and hunted, and praising Blucas's excellent performance. Jim McLennan of Girls With Guns, also awarding three stars, admired its gripping opening, the two lead performances and the tense scene with the hunters, but felt the middle section slack and the plotting, including a stranger who appears when needed, unconvincing.

A series of grisly murders is claiming the lives of young women in the city, and Captain Renfield assigns Detective Amelia Van Helsing to find the killer. All of the victims have red hair and are found drained of blood, with puncture wounds on their necks. The coroner, Jonathan Harker, suggests that the culprit may be something supernatural, an idea the rational Amelia initially dismisses. Meanwhile, Amelia's girlfriend Mina Murray has been promoted at work and is tasked with finding a property for a charming client, Count Dracula. As her investigation progresses, Amelia comes to believe that a vampire is responsible and realizes that it is Dracula, but the evidence points to a man who seems untouchable and who then disappears. The count is searching for the reincarnation of his long-lost love and has become fixated on Mina, convinced that she is the one. When Mina vanishes, Amelia is forced to question everything she believes, accept that monsters exist and confront the enigmatic count in a final showdown to save her.

The film was shot mainly in Belgrade, Serbia, and many supporting roles, including several of the vampire's victims, were filled by Serbian actors and models. It premiered in the United States on 28 January 2022 and was released in Germany on video on demand that July. Reviews were negative. Moria Reviews noted that the film never makes clear when and where it is set, since horses and carriages are heard but never seen and electric lighting alternates with candles, and remarked on the bold choice of making Van Helsing and Mina a lesbian couple. Writing for Voices from the Balcony, Jim Morazzini gave it one and a half stars out of five, criticizing a script that cannot decide between groan-worthy one-liners and serious vampire horror and calling Herbert one of the dullest Draculas he had seen, neither menacing nor charismatic.

During a punishing heatwave Claire Valens (Graham) has taken to sneaking into the pool of a luxury apartment building, where she meets the alluring Eve (Patterson) and is instantly drawn to her. A few nights later, out with Arlo Leonard (Wong), a police officer, she runs into Eve again at a bar, leaves Arlo and spends the night with her. At the Crane Corporation, the real estate company where she works, Claire suggests to its head Scott Crane (Roché) a derelict property ripe for redevelopment into apartments and hotels, and she is promoted to become his assistant, replacing Lane (Aren Buchholz). Invited to a party at Scott's home, she discovers that Eve is his wife. Claire tries to keep her distance, but Eve tells her she loves her and the affair resumes, until a colleague, Olivia (Kayla Wallace), sees them together. Scott storms out of the office, and when Claire goes to his house to talk to him, nobody is there.

Detective Parker (Cross) and Arlo arrive to investigate after blood is found at the Crane home. Pressured, Claire admits she was at the house, and once a hair of hers is found with Scott's blood, she becomes the prime suspect; warned by her friend Manuel (Andres Collantes), she goes on the run. Convinced that Eve has framed her, she sneaks into the Crane house to find proof. Meanwhile the police find the Cranes' ice pick in her apartment and Scott's burned body at the newly bought property, and Claire's past history with fire deepens their suspicion. Arlo, however, has doubts: he believes that Scott and Eve murdered Scott's previous wife and that Parker turned a blind eye. As the two search for evidence, Parker kills Arlo and overpowers Claire. Held captive at the abandoned site, Claire faces Eve, but when Parker asks Eve to kill her and she refuses, Lane steps forward as Scott's real killer, revealing that his true target was Claire, who as a teenager set the fire that killed his father. Claire escapes, sees Eve charged, and wins compensation from the police.

Sam (Duan), a young nurse, is assigned to care for a comatose patient (Conrad) at a remote, dark house in the English countryside, a job that leaves her alone with him through the night. As the hours pass she begins nosing around the house and uncovers a plot to unleash dark forces from within the human mind. Of those involved, her patient proved the most successful at reaching the malevolent entity, and as the night continues Sam finds herself terrorised by an unseen presence connected to him. Other characters include Dr. Carpenter (Read), Dr. Wright (Wood), Gwen (Secker), Joe (Blake) and a figure credited as the Old Hag (Nadif); the entity's full form is withheld until the final moments.

Writing on his horror review site MLMillerFrights, M. L. Miller called the film a wonderful mix of the coma horror classic Patrick and David Holroyd's The Haunted by way of Ti West's The House of the Devil. He praised the way it used the dark corners of the house to build a strong sense of foreboding even before the scares began, its subtle effects held back at the edges of the frame, and its tight, shadowy camerawork, and wrote that despite its very low budget the film enveloped the viewer with a sense of urgency. He found the dark entity genuinely frightening when it finally appeared, making the wait worthwhile, and concluded that Whisper told a fairly complex story with simple nuance and the familiar haunted-house play of shadow and light, to good effect.

Helen (Ayer) and her young-adult daughter Emily (Spruell), who constantly bicker, reluctantly accompany Helen's father Stan (Ward) on a camping trip in his RV, driving deep into the forest for a real outdoors experience. Soon after they settle in, an angry, armed landowner, Howard (Baldaramos), arrives and tells them they are trespassing and must move to public campsites ten miles away. As they try to leave, a wheel of the RV gets stuck in a hole, and Stan is seriously injured while trying to free it. With no mobile phone signal, Helen insists that the family stay together, and only the next morning sets off on foot for help. She comes upon Howard's isolated, dilapidated house and, finding the door unlocked, goes inside to look for a telephone. Instead she discovers a teenage boy, Andrew (Odette), chained to a bed in a locked room and screaming to be set free so that he can save his sister. Helen's assumptions about what is happening, and her choice whether to help him, have dangerous consequences for her family and for the boy's other keepers (Sharth and Winters) when they return, and she must fight to protect her family and escape the forest alive.

Reviews were largely negative. Dennis Harvey of Variety called the film a so-bad-it's-good candidate for drinking games, criticising its irritating, hapless protagonists, weak dialogue, clumsy action and draggy pacing, and noting that the explanation of events was relegated to a post-credits audio insert, though he credited some drone shots and Serpa's score. Bobby LePire of Film Threat gave it seven out of ten; despite calling Helen one of the year's most foolish characters, he felt the film found its footing once she sought help and praised a twist that subverted expectations.

Born and raised in Toronto, Williams taught himself cel animation and studied computer graphics at Sheridan College before ILM brought him from Canada in 1988 to animate the water tentacle in James Cameron's The Abyss. Cameron then gave him the job of supervising the morphing effects of the liquid metal T-1000 in Terminator 2: Judgment Day (1991). On Steven Spielberg's Jurassic Park, after being told that the dinosaurs would be created with traditional techniques, Williams made a computer-animated dinosaur test on his own time; when Kathleen Kennedy and Spielberg saw it, CGI moved to the center of the production. The film explores the mixed feelings of Williams and his colleagues about the revolution they unleashed, with Tippett lamenting how studios came to see CGI as a magic bullet that led to bloated spectacle, and it gives voice to Williams' long-held belief that superiors such as Tippett and Dennis Muren took credit for work he largely did. It also portrays him as a hard-drinking, abrasive rebel who clashed with ILM's corporate structure and damaged his career and relationships, and its final act shows him, after three stints in rehab, confronting his addiction and failures on camera, admitting that he has never been an adult.

The documentary was released in theaters and on video on demand in December 2022. Reviews were generally favorable. Matt Zoller Seitz of RogerEbert.com felt the film wavered between hero worship and critical distance and at times seemed unsure of its stance on CGI, but called its bleak, insightful final act strong enough to elevate the whole. Other critics praised its archival material and insight into effects history while noting that it was unevenly balanced.

The story unfolds in two timelines. In 1987, five teenagers in the town play Painkiller, a supernatural game using chess pieces, cards, a lighter and a timekeeper with a watch, in which each player describes a revenge fantasy and the one whose rage is purest is chosen to have their wish granted by an entity that feeds on pain, at a terrible cost. All of them die except Lea (Stiebitz), who is recorded on video saying that her friends are dead and that she may have killed them. In 2021, the peaceful town is shaken by a series of murders and suicides, the latest an old man shooting his best friend dead beside the lake, with chess pieces left at the scenes. Detective Tamara (Levesque) is assigned to investigate, to her annoyance, with a new partner, Lukas (Burlakov), who connects the case to the thirty-year-old footage. The inquiry strikes close to home: the grown-up Lea (Ferres), now blind and still haunted by the entity, is Tamara's mother, and she refuses to talk about the past. As the detectives try to understand the game's deadly myth before anyone else dies, the fraught relationship between mother and daughter comes to the fore.

Reviews were mixed. Road Rash gave it three stars, calling it an enjoyable, creepy film with Nordic noir undertones, attractive yet sinister Austrian scenery, good acting and a neat twist, though its flashbacks could be confusing and several plot points were left unexplained. Mihail Baltateanu of Grimoire of Horror praised it as one of the best-looking independent horror films of the year, with gorgeous wintry photography, but criticised its occasionally stilted dialogue and its reliance on on-screen pages of text as information dumps.

The documentary follows three main families. A lioness and her sisters are threatened when two young males challenge their ageing king; the usurpers destroy the harmony of the pride and cast her out, and, alone, she must hunt for herself and, after being made pregnant by a passing male, raise her cubs on her own. The alpha female of a pack of 24 painted wolves has trained her hunters to think and act as one, and the pack returns meat to its den to feed a litter of 14 pups. A six-month-old elephant calf experiences every challenge of Kalahari life for the first time within her herd, guided by a matriarch who remembers vital water sources. As drought grips the region, these animals and great numbers of wildebeest, giraffes, zebras, hippos and buffalo converge on the delta. When floodwaters from rain that fell months earlier in the Angolan Highlands finally arrive, the landscape becomes a lush wetland, a boon for grazers but a hardship for the hunters, as the water-adapted lechwe easily escape the wolves. By September the water is receding, and by October the delta is a scorching dust bowl where the balance of power shifts back to the predators, lightning ignites fires and swarms of locusts emerge, until the elephants, able to detect distant thunder, sense the coming of the rains.

Reviews were positive. Johnny Loftus of Decider recommended streaming it, praising the way it linked the experiences of the young animals to the wisdom of their elders, its visceral predation scenes, such as the lioness bringing down a wildebeest alone, and its excellent camerawork and drone photography. Aaron Phillips of But Why Tho? gave it 9 out of 10, calling it wholesome and enthralling, and singling out Page's soft-spoken, eloquent narration, the score and the cinematography, which he felt shaped the footage into an evocative story.

In a small Texas lake town, Spencer Timms is a hard-drinking game warden whose alcoholism has cost him his family; he wakes up hours late, fills a thermos with coffee and vodka and heads to work. His dim friend Nolan shows him a shark he has caught and plans to sell for its teeth, and Spencer tells him to get rid of it so that no one thinks there are sharks in the lake. Too lazy to dispose of it properly, Nolan dumps it in the water, but the bull shark, a species able to live in both salt and fresh water, is not dead, and it soon devours a young woman swimming in the lake. When her remains are found with a shark's tooth lodged in her back, the sheriff and the mayor, facing an election year and fearful for the summer tourist season, want the matter settled quickly and quietly, and the mayor's office pressures the coroner over her report. While the shark claims more victims, Spencer struggles with his drinking, his wife serves him with divorce papers and his teenage son comes to stay. After the sheriff is killed by the shark and Grant is attacked in the water, Spencer and Dottie, with C-4 explosives supplied by Nolan, take a boat onto the lake to destroy the animal, though a final shot reveals another shark in the water.

ITN released the film free with advertisements on Tubi and YouTube, as well as on DVD and other streaming platforms. Reviews were mixed. Jim Morazzini of Voices from the Balcony and Nerdly gave it 3 out of 5, describing it as Jaws relocated to a Texas lake with added domestic drama and comic relief, and finding it entertaining despite few attacks and variable computer-generated effects. Jim McLennan of Film Blitz enjoyed its laid-back tone, which he likened to Lake Placid, but called the climax embarrassingly flat, while Jamie Tingle of The Daily Jaws considered it so bad it was good.

Salvador Campodónico (Iglesias), a workaholic Spanish architect whose family owns Spain's leading hotel company, travels to Cusco to lead his first international project, a luxury hotel, although his father Alberto (Vicente Vergara) doubts he is ready for such a responsibility. He wanders into the lively hostel next door, run by Lichi (Wendy Ramos), and meets her niece Ariana (Cayo), a free-spirited, fiery artist who lives a life opposite to his. The morning after they spend the night together, Ariana learns that he intends to build the hotel on land that includes her aunt's hostel, and she is furious. To understand her world, Salvador persuades her to guide him through the region, and the trip through Inca sites and landscapes brings them closer. On the bus back, a violent storm triggers a panic attack in Ariana, and Lichi tells Salvador that Ariana was the sole survivor of a car accident that killed her parents when she was thirteen. Pressed by his father and his board to close the deal and persuade Lichi to sell, Salvador hesitates to commit, and Ariana leaves without telling anyone where she is going. Salvador sets out to find Ariana, tells her he has left the company to take a year off and that the project will not go ahead, and the two reunite.

Conceived by Ascenzo around 2013 as a travel film, the project was announced in February 2020 when Netflix's Reed Hastings visited Lima. Delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic, it was shot from March to May 2021 under the working title Mochileros in Cusco, Puno and Paracas. It topped Netflix's charts in Peru and reached second place among the platform's most-watched non-English films in its first full week. Reviews were mixed: critics praised its landscapes and photography but found the script, characters and humour thin, with several likening it to a tourism advertisement and others criticising the lack of indigenous representation.

Mel, a talented 26-year-old IT security expert in Rotterdam, is auditing the software that controls the country's first self-driving bus for the transport company Rotramax. The system processes images of passengers' faces to allow secure payment, and Mel discovers that this biometric data is secretly being sent to outside recipients. To stop the leak, she plants her own Trojan, unknowingly making herself the target of an international criminal network. Two armed men break into her apartment and chase her; when she escapes to a police station, she sees them chatting amiably with officers and flees again. She is helped by Thomas, the man she met the night before on a failed blind date. Soon a video appears on television apparently showing Mel shooting a man, and she becomes a fugitive. A man named Rogers offers to make her "video problem" disappear if she decrypts the Trojan, threatening Thomas as well. To prove that the footage is a deepfake, Mel turns to the eccentric Buddy, a former partner she once reported for keeping money they had seized from criminals. Their search leads to a facial-recognition company working with Rotramax that steals personal data, and Mel realizes the fake video was built from data captured when she boarded the bus. After Rogers's men kill Buddy, Mel breaks into the Rotramax server room, where a shootout cuts the link to the driverless bus on its maiden trip with fifteen passengers aboard. With Thomas's help on board, she stops the bus before it plunges toward an opened bridge, clears her name and inherits a digital network Buddy built.

Filming lasted two months, partly in Rotterdam, where the Erasmus Bridge was closed to traffic for night shoots. Released on Netflix on 1 November 2022, the film drew largely negative reviews, with critics citing clichéd plotting, flat dialogue and limited budget in the final action scenes, though some praised Brood. It nonetheless became an international hit, ranking second among Netflix's non-English films worldwide in its first week with more than 25 million hours viewed.

Jess (Smith) is still haunted by the drowning of her mother a decade earlier, and her memories of near-drownings recur throughout the film. Estranged from her father, whom she resents for starting a new relationship, and desperate to escape her small seaside town, she sets out to party with friends and meets Ben (Daddario), a charming, attractive visitor who promises a romantic escape and who, like her, has lost a parent. After a whirlwind night together, Jess wakes up on Ben's boat to find that he has taken them out to sea. Despite her initial misgivings, she embraces the carefree domestic life he seems to offer. The idyll unravels when a stranger, Lexie (Alexander), crashes her jet ski into the side of the boat and comes aboard. Lexie and Ben accuse each other of vicious lies and dark secrets, and in the cramped, claustrophobic quarters of the boat a dangerous cat-and-mouse game develops, forcing Jess to decide whom to believe as deceit, mistrust and violence escalate and she must fight for her own survival.

Critical reception was negative. Rachel LaBonte of Screen Rant gave the film two out of five stars, finding that it showed moments of promise and created a genuine mystery once Lexie's motives emerged, with the boat setting used to claustrophobic effect and capable performances from the three leads, but that it lacked suspense, asked viewers to forgive implausible behaviour and ended with a twist that strained credulity. Alan French of Sunshine State Cineplex rated it three out of ten, criticising poorly written exchanges, wooden performances and an unsympathetic heroine, and objecting that the film flirted with troubling ideas about guilt and trauma before backtracking on them in the final act.

The documentary follows Díaz from a childhood of extreme poverty and his early struggle to make a name for himself in the competitive world of vallenato to his rise as a superstar in the 1980s and 1990s, whose songs drew on his own experiences and filled concerts with huge crowds. It portrays an exuberant, impulsive figure with a famous smile and a diamond set in his tooth, who boasted of fathering dozens of children with many women and whose drinking and drug use grew alongside increasingly chaotic shows. The second half turns to May 1997, when Niño, who had met Díaz at a concert and had a relationship with him, went to his Bogotá apartment and never returned home; her body was found the next morning in a cow pasture near Tunja. The film examines the conflicting accounts of that night, the investigation that connected Díaz and members of his entourage to her death, her brother's efforts to defend her reputation, Díaz's denials, his flight from justice and the trial in which he was convicted of involuntary manslaughter. It leaves viewers to weigh the competing versions for themselves.

The documentary was released on Netflix on 30 March 2022. Romey Norton of Ready Steady Cut considered it a good, intriguing watch, praising its energetic Colombian music, quick cutting and contrasting cinematography, and its wide range of interviewees, including the victim's brother, whose determination she found moving. Pooja Sharma of Leisurebyte called it a gripping and thorough account of an icon whose story had been curiously under-told, presenting it as the sad tale of a man so consumed by fame that he lost sight of everything else. Díaz died of a heart attack in Valledupar at the age of 56, days after releasing his thirtieth album.

Jeff Mitchell (Pohlkamp) appears to have it all: an interesting, well-paid job, a loving wife, Lisa (Castles), and two children, the caring Noah (Jarrah) and the mildly rebellious Ella (Morrow). When his talented colleague Blake (Taylor) is promoted over him to replace their boss, Jeff goes to a bar to consider his next steps. There a young woman, Carlee Byrne (Foster), introduces herself; he mistakes her approach for flirtation, but she asks whether he remembers Jennifer, his high-school girlfriend, and reveals that Jennifer became pregnant by him without his knowledge, moved away and raised her daughter alone, never telling her who her father was. Jennifer's recent death in an accident has prompted Carlee to seek the truth. Stunned, Jeff and Lisa ask her to take a paternity test; when the results appear to confirm that she is his daughter, Jeff welcomes her into the family. Ella, however, does not trust her, and she is right: Carlee is dangerous and willing to kill to secure a perfect family. To protect her secret she fakes lab results, poisons a man and commits murder, and when Ella's boyfriend Ryan (Gran) tries to catch her in a lie, she warns him off with a knife at his throat.

Reviews were mixed. Phil Wheat of Nerdly described the film as another riff on Single White Female that followed a very familiar formula but was too clean-cut and watered down to make an impact; he found Morrow's tenacious, genuine performance as Ella the only real standout, considered Foster's Carlee too two-dimensional to be an intriguing villain and criticised the weak ending, though he suggested fans of home-invasion thrillers might enjoy it. That Darn Girl Movie Reviews gave it three out of five stars, calling it entertaining though predictable, describing Carlee as a worthy foe for Ella and singling out her chilling exchanges with Ryan.

Five young friends are enjoying their last spring break before graduation at a beach resort in Mexico. After a night of drinking and partying, during which the cautious Nat, the only one who speaks Spanish, ignores a local amputee's warning about what lurks in the water, the group steals two jet skis early in the morning and races them out to sea. A reckless game of chicken ends in a head-on collision: one machine is left capsized and abandoned, Greg suffers a badly broken leg, and the five end up crowded onto a single stalled jet ski drifting farther from shore. Because the craft were taken without permission while nobody was around, no one knows they are missing, and their only slim hope is that someone notices when they fail to board their flight home. Tensions boil over when it emerges that Milly slept with Tom behind Nat's back the night before. Tyler, despite a head injury, tries to swim for help, but a great white shark begins circling, and the predator toys with the survivors one by one as they search for a way to save themselves, leaving Nat to fight for her life in the final stretch.

Shark Bait was released in the United States on 13 May 2022 and on DVD and digital platforms in the United Kingdom on 6 June 2022. Reviews were mixed to negative. Jennie Kermode of Eye for Film was the most positive, praising an opening that pays intelligent tribute to Jaws, convincing shark footage, effective action and a predator presented as an animal with a mind of its own. Blueprint: Review found it handsome and well made, with a standout turn from Earl, but faulted its thin plot, unlikable characters and needless melodrama. In The Guardian, Phil Hoad gave it a scathing review, calling it a depressingly unimaginative thriller that lacks tension compared with Open Water or The Shallows and joking that the shark had more charisma than the cast.

Travelling by train to Central City, Ed and Al meet Ling Yao (Keisuke Watanabe), a prince from Xing seeking the secret of immortality. When bandits hijack the train, the brothers fight them on the locomotive, are unexpectedly helped by the homunculus Envy, and use alchemy to stop a bomb plot. In Central they learn that a serial killer is murdering State Alchemists. Slipping away from their bodyguards, they meet May Chang, a girl from Xing, and are attacked by Scar, an Ishvalan who badly damages Al's armour and destroys Ed's automail arm before Mustang drives him off. While Ed returns to Resembool for repairs, he encounters his estranged father Van Hohenheim (Seiyo Uchino), and Scar recovers among Ishvalan refugees. Ling proposes an alliance to capture Scar and the homunculi, but the trap collapses: Winry learns that Scar killed her parents, a doctor couple, during the Ishval war and tries to shoot him, King Bradley (Hiroshi Tachi) wounds Ling's bodyguard Lan Fan, and Scar escapes with May. Riza Hawkeye tells Ed about the massacre of Ishval, in which Scar lost his brother. Later, when Al and May find Scar, Winry dresses his wound and he expresses remorse. In a final clash, the homunculus Gluttony swallows Ed, Ling and Envy, and inside his stomach Envy reveals that Gluttony is a failed Gate of Truth created by Father before transforming into a monstrous dragon.

The ensemble also includes Yuina Kuroshima as Lan Fan, Ron Monroe as May, Kokoro Terada as Selim Bradley, Yuki Yamada as Kimblee, Kanata Hongo as Envy and Jun Fubuki as Pinako Rockbell.

Edward escapes from inside the homunculus Gluttony and, at the Gate of Truth, finds Alphonse's real body, which refuses to leave without its soul. Mustang and Hawkeye discover that King Bradley is the homunculus Wrath and that the military's generals are complicit, while the brothers learn that Father, a being who resembles Hohenheim, plans to open the Gate using a nationwide transmutation circle drawn by wars the army has orchestrated. Ed travels to the northern fortress of Briggs to seek General Olivier Armstrong's help, and Al finds their father, who reveals his past as a slave whose blood created a homunculus in a flask; that creature sacrificed the people of the ancient kingdom of Xerxes to gain a body and immortality. The heroes, joined by Scar, Ling and his possessed alter ego Greed, descend beneath Central City for a final confrontation. Father absorbs the souls of the country but is thwarted by Hohenheim, and in the ensuing battle Al sacrifices himself to restore his brother's arm. Ed defeats Father, then gives up his own alchemy to bring Al back whole, and the brothers return home to Winry.

The two-part finale was announced in March 2022 as part of the manga's 20th anniversary. Filming was originally planned in Italy, like the first film, but because of the COVID-19 pandemic it took place on an open set built in Kyonan, Chiba Prefecture. The Final Alchemy was released in Japanese theaters on 24 June 2022, five weeks after The Revenge of Scar, and became available worldwide on Netflix on 24 September 2022.

The film opens at Lopez's family party for her 50th birthday in July 2019 and follows her over the next six months. Behind the scenes, it tracks the awards campaign for Hustlers, which brought her the strongest reviews of her career after years of popular but critically derided comedies and her first Golden Globe nomination since Selena, along with her hopes for a first Academy Award nomination, which ultimately does not come. In parallel, it shows her preparing the halftime show of 2 February 2020 with her music director and choreographers, frustrated at having to share the brief slot with Shakira, and fighting the network executives to keep a segment with children in cages as a statement about the treatment of migrants at the border, a battle she wins. Glimpses of the past include her debut as a Fly Girl on In Living Color, her breakthrough in Selena, the video for "Waiting for Tonight" and her decision to wear again the Versace dress that caused a sensation at the 2000 Grammy Awards. She also reflects on the intense tabloid scrutiny of her private life, the obstacles she has faced as a Latina, and her views on the politics of the Trump era. The film closes with her performance at the inauguration of Joe Biden. Interviewees include Ben Affleck, Shakira, Hustlers director Lorene Scafaria, Constance Wu and Julia Stiles.

Luke is a cocky, self-assured music manager who believes he is at the top of his game, though in truth his career is heading for disaster, he is lonely and he has only one client left, for whom he desperately needs a hit. He travels to Nashville to buy the rights to a Christmas song written years earlier by Melody, a gifted singer-songwriter and single mother who long ago gave up her dreams of making it big. Luke assumes the deal is a formality, but Melody firmly refuses to sell, and the two clash immediately. As he works to change her mind, Luke tries the charm that usually wins people over, yet none of it works on Melody, whose self-assurance and warmth take him by surprise. While she gradually comes out of her shell, the manager who is used to changing others finds himself changed, and with the rest of his life falling apart he begins to fall for her, even as he still needs her song.

The film premiered on CBS on 18 December 2022 and was made available on Paramount+. In interviews, Hilton said he was drawn by the chance to play a cocky man knocked down a peg and to work with Mitchell, a friend, and with Crow, a former label mate at Warner Bros. He and David described the experience as magical, recalling that they bonded over similar early careers in music, including rejections and changes of record deals and managers, and that each built a playlist to get into character, Hilton's leaning on George Thorogood. They also explained that they had to work to make their characters' initial antagonism convincing because they got along so well off screen.

The story opens on a dramatic night when both Tristan and Célène appear close to despair, with Tristan narrating that fame is power in the modern age, before flashing back to show how they got there. In Biarritz, Célène, a shy and studious seventeen-year-old who prefers literature to social media and is in a long-distance relationship, is starting at a new school, Victor Hugo High. There she meets Tristan, a champion surfer with 3.5 million Instagram followers, after he saves her dog from being run over by a driver livestreaming at the wheel. Tristan and Vanessa, the pampered child star of a film series who is afraid of becoming a has-been, present themselves online as a couple, but their relationship is a sham; the two cynics actually enjoy scheming to destroy other people's romances. Unaware that she is the object of a cruel bet between them, Célène falls for Tristan as he sets out to seduce her, manipulating those around her, including her friend Tao, a DJ and dealer, and her goofy cousin Charlotte. Preparations for the school musical, a costume party with spiked punch and a surfing lesson that ends in a romantic beach hut push the scheme forward, while Célène, who joins Instagram under a provocative handle, gradually discovers the power and cruelty of online fame.

Released on Netflix on 8 July 2022, the film drew mostly negative reviews. Decider's John Serba advised viewers to skip it, calling it a toothless social-media remake that pales beside the 1988 Stephen Frears film and Cruel Intentions, with a soft Tristan, an underwritten heroine and a drawn-out ending, though he praised Janjaud's spirited comic performance and the idea behind Vanessa's character. The New York Times and Firstpost likewise found its social-media update colorful but shallow and clichéd.

The world is in an alarming state: famines caused by global warming, a new pandemic fueled by antibiotic resistance and escalating violence and unrest across the globe, followed by storms, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes and swarms of locusts. More and more world leaders fear that the cascade of disasters signals the coming apocalypse and the end of days. At the Pentagon, Norris is ordered to assemble a small team of specialists, Hughes, Lenna and Rodney, who are sent with a military peacekeeping force under the deeply religious Major Jones to the apparent epicenter of the catastrophes, a lake region in Brazil. Working from an abandoned observatory, the scientists determine that the eruptions originate beneath a central lake and are setting off a chain reaction around the world. Racing to learn whether the disaster can be stopped, and whether it is supernatural, Rodney improvises homemade bombs designed to wipe out the locust swarms by disrupting their oxygen, to be detonated by a gunshot fired from a moving helicopter, while others attempt to seal the volcanic lake by crashing a helicopter into it. Meanwhile, a fungus released by the volcano causes soldiers who inhale it to hallucinate and turn violent, and Jones believes he sees the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse riding across the sky.

Filmed in California, the film was released on video on demand in the United States on 29 April 2022 and reached German video stores that September. Reviews were poor. Moria Reviews gave it two stars, finding the concept awkwardly handled, with the supposed end of the world reduced to events around a single Brazilian lake, though it enjoyed the brief computer-generated glimpses of the Horsemen and Roche's inventive pseudo-scientific schemes. Film-rezensionen.de awarded it two out of ten, calling it boring because of its drawn-out dialogue, criticizing its failure to engage with the biblical background and calling it a typical cheap Asylum production.

Natalie Wolf (Lapira) is an acclaimed author of Christmas love stories who is herself unlucky in love and has lived as a recluse since being burned by a journalist years earlier. Struggling with her latest novel, she follows her editor's advice to list the five qualities she wants in a partner and to get out and experience the world, agreeing to a book signing near Buffalo, her first public appearance in six years, on condition that she speaks to no journalists. Nick Winters (Bledsoe), a reporter for the magazine SHE, needs a major cover story to boost sales and stave off a merger with a rival publication, and sees the elusive author as the answer. Natalie recognises that he is no fan and rebuffs him. When a blizzard strands them both in the small town of Cranberry Falls, Natalie is stunned to be rescued by the tow-truck driver Caleb (Witte), her high-school crush and the model for the hero of her current book, who has organised the town's annual Dickens Festival, commemorating a stay by Charles Dickens at the local inn, and its toy drive. Joined by his photographer Lucas (Collins), a devoted fan of Natalie's books who begins a romance with her publicist Ryan (Beauchesne), Nick decides to chronicle her reunion with the one who got away without her help, only to find himself falling for her.

Reviews were favourable. Decider recommended streaming it, observing that the film began as a formulaic holiday romance but stood out by adding a love triangle, a second romance and Natalie's imagined scenes from her novels, playfully expanding the genre's conventions, and crediting its charming performers. Steve Gidlow of MediaVillage called it a refreshing take on a familiar story thanks to strong lead performances, and Lapira said she enjoyed playing a character far less self-assured than her role in The Equalizer.

Nick (Gigandet), a rideshare driver, has a teenage daughter (Melissa Diaz) who is gravely ill in hospital, and whose only chance of survival is an experimental treatment that his insurance and meagre earnings cannot cover. Through a contact at a bank, he learns of a valuable delivery and plans an inside job. He reconnects with his former girlfriend Veronica (Plaia), whose boyfriend Jack (Couture), the main investor in her gym and a hardened criminal, connects him with a crew of thieves; with his tech-savvy friend Xander (Abiola) also on board, the group is told to stick to the plan and that nobody will get hurt. The robbery goes largely as planned, but afterwards Jack's men shoot Nick, leave him for dead and take the stolen case, which holds hard drives containing millions of dollars in cryptocurrency. Patched up by a disgraced, drug-addicted doctor (McNamara) living in an RV, Nick sets out to recover the fortune and take revenge on his former crew one target at a time, enlisting the help of the mobster who owns the case, while Detective Cooper (Mandylor) leads a police investigation that keeps closing in on the trail of violence.

Reviews were generally negative. Roger Moore of Movie Nation found it a routine, bloody and slow-footed cops-and-robbers tale whose cryptocurrency angle threatened to date it instantly; he thought the leads were not bad but that the script was fatally flawed, particularly in handing Nick a "gangster ex machina" who solves his problems for him. Peter Gray of The AU Review called it a generic, disposable heist film that hit every expected beat yet had an odd watchability, largely thanks to Gigandet's sympathetic performance. Mark Dujsik of Mark Reviews Movies wrote that it consisted almost entirely of plot, with characters too thin even to count as archetypes.
